title: Listening Skills Training in Serbia
text:
Waitlist-controlled field experiment for social workers
    Listening Skills Training in Serbia

    • 20 Serbian municipalities (10 experimental, 10 control)
    • Four measurement occasions (T0–T3, January–December)
    • 451 social workers
    • 102 items & 23 preregistered scales
    • Three hypothesis blocks (H1 Listening & Togetherness → H2 Cognitive Complexity → H3 Well-being)

  

  
    Start
    
      
        Read me
        What this report documents and what each chapter holds.
        →
      
    
  

  
    Part A — Data
    
      
        From Questionnaires to the Analysis File
        79 Excel files, code corrections, double entries, and the case log.
        →
      
      
        Scales and Analysis Datasets
        Reverse coding, scale composites, long and wide data.
        →
      
      
        Sample
        Participants, waves, municipalities, and sample sets.
        →
      
      
        Data Quality
        Careless responding, two flags, and the search for double entries.
        →
      
    
  

  
    Part B — Measurement
    
      
        Reliability and Baseline Correlations
        Reliability per wave and correlations at baseline.
        →
      
      
        Measurement Models per Wave
        Confirmatory factor models at each wave (T0–T3).
        →
      
      
        Measurement Invariance over Time
        Configural, metric, and scalar invariance across the waves.
        →
      
      
        Simultaneous Block Models
        Block CFAs: discriminant validity and block-level invariance.
        →
      
    
  

  
    Part C — Training Effects (Preregistered)
    
      
        Means and Δd
        Means by condition and wave, and standardized change.
        →
      
      
        Multilevel Models
        Treatment effects, replication, and sensitivity.
        →
      
      
        Latent Difference-in-Differences
        Latent DiD in structured means models.
        →
      
      
        Serial Mediation
        Serial mediation chain: H1 → H2 → H3.
        →
      
      
        Movers
        Classification of individual change.
        →
      
      
        Robustness across Sample Sets
        The training effects on the sample sets S0 to S9.
        →
      
    
  

  
    Part D — Post Hoc
    
      
        Item Pruning
        Reduction and cleanup of the item pool.
        →
      
      
        Exploratory Graph Analysis
        Dimensional structure via network psychometrics.
        →
      
      
        Redundancy & IRT
        Redundancy analysis (UVA) and graded response models.
        →
      
      
        Final Structure
        The final item pool, its communities, factors and composites.
        →
      
      
        Training Effects on the New Structure
        Δd, multilevel models and mediation on the two factors.
        →
      
      
        Synthesis
        Integration of all findings.
        →
      
    
  

  
    Part E — Appendix
    
      
        Item-Level Δd
        The training effects item by item, ranked.
        →
      
      
        Software Versions
        R, Quarto and every package with its version.
        →
      
      
        Requests and Their Status
        What the team asked for, in plain words, and where it stands.
        →

title: 0. Read me
text:
What each chapter contains
Part A: Data

From questionnaires to the analysis file. Reads the 79 Excel files returned by the municipalities, builds the participant codes, corrects codes that were mistyped, removes paper forms that were entered twice, and saves one analysis file.
Scales and analysis datasets. Reverse-codes negatively worded items, builds the 23 scale scores and the three hypothesis composites, and arranges the data one row per questionnaire and one row per person.
Sample. Who took part, at which waves and in which municipalities; whether the two conditions are comparable; the sample sets used to test robustness.
Data quality. Screens every questionnaire for careless responding and searches once more for forms entered twice.

Part B: Measurement

Reliability and baseline correlations. Internal consistency of every scale and composite at each wave, and how the scales relate before the training.
Measurement models per wave. Confirmatory factor analysis of every scale at each of the four waves.
Measurement invariance over time. Whether each scale measures the same construct in the same way at all four waves, the precondition for comparing means over time; judged by two sets of cutoffs, with partial invariance, approximate invariance (alignment) and a test across the two groups before the training.
Simultaneous block models. All scales of one hypothesis modelled together, to test whether they are distinct.

Part C: Training effects, as preregistered

Means and Δd. Means by condition and wave, and the standardized difference in change between the trained and the waiting group, with a second standard deviation, a correction for multiple testing and a look at dropout.
Multilevel models. The preregistered models of the training effect, with participants nested in municipalities and, as a check, in trainers; one-sided tests and a correction for multiple testing; the replication in the second round; random slopes; equivalence tests.
Latent difference-in-differences. The training effect on latent means, corrected for measurement error; with the control group’s change while it waits, a correction for multiple testing, a restricted model and the effects across the sample sets.
Serial mediation. Whether the training improves well-being through listening and cognitive complexity, with manifest composites and with latent blocks.
Movers. How many participants changed reliably, by condition.
Robustness. Every effect re-estimated in alternative samples: complete cases, attrition patterns, careless responding.

Part D: Post hoc

Item pruning. Which items were set aside, for ceiling effects or low responsiveness, and why.
Exploratory graph analysis. The dimensional structure of the item pool, estimated from the data.
Redundancy and IRT. Redundant items and item response models, also at each wave.
Final structure. The resulting item structure and its replication across the four waves.
Training effects on the new structure. The training effects re-estimated on the factors found in the data and on the single item on life satisfaction, and whether the factors are measured invariantly over time.
Synthesis. How the preregistered and the post hoc results fit together.

Part E: Appendix

Study 1. The train-the-trainer study with the 16 trainers; it follows once its data are available.
Item-level Δd. The training effect on every single item.
Software versions.
Requests and their status. What the team asked for in its e-mails, in plain words, and where each request stands.

title: 0. Read me
text:
The study
What was studied? Social workers in 20 Serbian municipalities took part in a listening training. Ten municipalities were trained between January and March 2025; the other ten waited and were trained between September and December 2025. Participants answered the same questionnaire up to four times: in January (T0), March (T1), September (T2) and December (T3). The analyses test whether the training improved listening and togetherness (H1), cognitive complexity (H2) and well-being (H3).

title: 0. Read me
text:
How to read this report
How do code and results relate?

Every chapter shows the code that produces its results, directly above them. Code that several chapters share is kept in a separate file and shown in full where it is used.
The text explains each step in plain language. Knowing R helps, but the logic can be followed without it.
Each chapter names the tables and sections of the paper its results feed.
Numbers that the paper reports are checked in the code: a hidden line stops the report if one of them changes.

How is each chapter built? The same way throughout. Section 1 of a chapter lists the steps that every unit of the chapter goes through (a construct, an outcome, a model, a processing step) and the criteria that decide each step, with a diagram of the path. Section 2 shows the data and the helper functions used for checks, figures and summary tables; the analyses themselves are written out where they happen. Then each unit follows under its own heading. It opens with its path through the steps: a table of each step’s question and result. The steps are grouped into parts, which the table of contents on the left shows; a label beside each step names the data it uses, and each step ends by naming the next. Every step runs the same way: a question, the code that answers it, its output and what it means. Before a model is read, it goes through the checks that the textbooks of its method name; in Chapters 7, 8 and 11 a model that fails them stops. The last section of each chapter sets all units side by side.
Can the analyses be re-run? The questionnaires carry self-generated participant codes, ages and sex, so the data are not published with this report. The code is complete: every step can be followed and applied to comparable data.
Who is SW0123? Every person appears under a pseudonym: the respondent ID of the data deposit (SW0001 to SW0461, and SW0462 for the second of two people who shared one code), or T01 to T64 for a code that was typed at one wave and corrected later. The codes themselves, built from the mother’s name and birthday, never appear in this report.

title: 1. From Questionnaires to the Analysis File
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



How the 79 Excel files of the municipalities become one analysis file, in ten processing steps: reading the questionnaires, building the participant codes, replacing them by pseudonyms, correcting mistyped codes, the corrections made for this report (codes joined, a code split, paper forms entered twice), keeping one questionnaire per person and wave, turning the answers into numbers, setting impossible answers to missing, marking the waves each person attended, and saving the file without the codes. Each processing step is shown in the same six steps, and every correction is listed with its evidence; a table at the end puts all processing steps side by side. Feeds the description of the sample and of data processing in the Method section, and the table of deviations from the preregistration.

title: 1. From Questionnaires to the Analysis File
text:
1.1 Reading the questionnaires
What did the municipalities send? One Excel file per municipality and wave. Twenty municipalities and four waves would make 80 files; three waves never arrived (Lebane in March, Sokobanja and Valjevo in December), and Leskovac and Užice sent their December questionnaires in two files each: 79 files.

# The questionnaires: one Excel file per municipality and wave
# -> one row per questionnaire

# one fixed order on every computer: where a code leaves age or sex blank at
# one wave, it is filled from the questionnaire read first
excel_files <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.xlsx$", full.names = TRUE) |>
  str_subset("/~\\$", negate = TRUE) |>   # not the lock files of open workbooks
  stri_sort(locale = "en_US")

if (length(excel_files) != 79) {
  stop("Expected the 79 Excel files in '", raw_dir, "', found ",
       length(excel_files), " (see data/README.md).", call. = FALSE)
}

# One file: the answers below three label rows (Serbian wording, an empty
# row, English wording), municipality and wave from the file name, e.g.
# "Arilje - Trainee Questionnaires - December 2025", empty rows dropped.
read_questionnaires <- \(file) {
  name  <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))
  month <- months_list[str_detect(name, regex(months_list, ignore_case = TRUE))]
  answers <- read_excel(file, .name_repair = "unique_quiet") |>
    mutate(across(where(is.character), enc2utf8)) |>
    slice(-(1:3)) |>
    mutate(Municipality = sub("Trainees.*", "", sub("^(.*?)-.*", "\\1", name)),
           Occasion     = month[1])
  answers[rowSums(is.na(answers)) < ncol(answers) - 2, ]
}

raw <- excel_files |>
  map(read_questionnaires) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(sex          = toupper(trimws(sex)),
         age          = as.numeric(age),
         Municipality = trimws(Municipality),
         Occasion     = trimws(Occasion))

# five files carry notes of the data entry in an unnamed extra column
entry_notes <- raw |>
  filter(!is.na(`...111`)) |>
  select(Municipality, Occasion, note = `...111`)

raw <- raw |> select(-`...111`)

1.4 Corrections made for this report
What did the checks of 2026 add? Four lists. The paper forms were not available, so every entry rests on the data; the evidence follows the lists.

# Corrections made for this report (November 2026); the evidence for each is
# shown in Chapter 1

# one person, two codes -> joined under one ID (the ID of the person joined)
code_merges <- tribble(
  ~municipality, ~code_from, ~code_to, ~source,
  # the code written a second time, at the end, names a person with other waves
  "Arilje",      "SW0163",   "SW0283", "second code entry",
  "Požarevac",   "SW0374",   "SW0368", "second code entry",
  "Raška",       "SW0397",   "SW0351", "second code entry",
  "NoviPazar",   "SW0186",   "SW0327", "second code entry",
  "Valjevo",     "SW0323",   "SW0353", "second code entry",
  # the Serbian letter Lj typed as "LJ" at one wave, as "L" at the others
  "Arilje",      "SW0250",   "SW0440", "spelling",
  "Sokobanja",   "SW0326",   "SW0167", "spelling",
  "Sokobanja",   "SW0160",   "SW0190", "spelling",
  # a Cyrillic A (U+0410), which looks like the Latin A of the other waves
  "Pirot",       "SW0312",   "SW0053", "spelling",
  # the day of birth left blank at one wave; same month, age and sex
  "Vršac",       "SW0408",   "SW0090", "missing day"
)

# two people, one code: round 5 joined T08 onto SW0337 and so put two
# January questionnaires on one person -> the second gets an own ID
code_splits <- tribble(
  ~code,    ~Occasion, ~age, ~new_code,
  "SW0337", 0,         54,   "SW0462"
)

# one paper form, entered twice -> the later entry is removed
double_entries <- tribble(
  ~code,    ~Occasion, ~same_form_as_code, ~same_form_as_occasion,
  "SW0206", 1,         "SW0206",           0,
  "SW0082", 3,         "SW0082",           2,
  "SW0402", 3,         "SW0402",           2,
  "SW0002", 3,         "SW0002",           2,
  "SW0210", 3,         "SW0210",           2,
  "SW0284", 3,         "SW0284",           2,
  "SW0225", 3,         "SW0225",           2,
  "SW0359", 3,         "SW0359",           2,
  "SW0208", 3,         "SW0208",           2,
  "SW0165", 1,         "SW0165",           0,
  "SW0209", 1,         "SW0209",           0,
  "SW0083", 3,         "SW0040",           2     # under a mistyped code
)

# answers outside the scale from 0 to 10, both in one December
# questionnaire -> missing (after the answers become numbers, 1.6)
out_of_range <- tribble(
  ~code,    ~Occasion, ~item,             ~value,
  "SW0385", 3,         "ParadoxMindset7", 20,
  "SW0385", 3,         "ParadoxMindset8", 20
)


Evidence

items <- names(select(x, ListenOther1:needSatisfaction24))

# Share of answers (in %) in which two questionnaires agree, counted over the
# items answered in both. Copies of one paper form agree in almost all answers.
share_identical <- \(a, b) {
  round(100 * mean(unlist(a[1, items]) == unlist(b[1, items]), na.rm = TRUE))
}

# One line per person: waves, age and sex.
describe_persons <- \(ids) {
  x |>
    filter(code %in% ids) |>
    summarise(waves = paste0("T", sort(unique(Occasion)), collapse = ", "),
              age   = paste(unique(age), collapse = "/"),
              sex   = paste(unique(sex), collapse = "/"),
              .by = code)
}

# Two persons' codes compared without showing them, on their first
# questionnaires: the parts that differ (letter, month, day), and whether the
# code written a second time, at the end of the first person's
# questionnaire, is the second person's code ("blank" if left empty).
compare_codes <- \(from, to) {
  a <- x |> filter(code == from) |> slice(1)
  b <- x |> filter(code == to) |> slice(1)
  start_a <- as.character(c(a$`Letter...1`, a$`Month...2`, a$`Day...3`))
  start_b <- as.character(c(b$`Letter...1`, b$`Month...2`, b$`Day...3`))
  end_a   <- as.character(c(a$`Letter...108`, a$`Month...109`, a$`Day...110`))
  differs <- c("letter", "month", "day")[!map2_lgl(start_a, start_b, identical)]
  tibble(parts_differ     = paste(differs, collapse = " and "),
         end_names_joined = case_when(all(is.na(end_a))        ~ "blank",
                                      identical(end_a, start_b) ~ "yes",
                                      TRUE                      ~ "no"))
}

For comparison: how far do one person’s answers agree between two waves? Over everyone who answered in March and in September, the median share:

both_waves <- intersect(x$code[x$Occasion == 1], x$code[x$Occasion == 2])

both_waves |>
  map_dbl(\(id) share_identical(filter(x, code == id, Occasion == 1),
                                filter(x, code == id, Occasion == 2))) |>
  median()

            by = c(code_to = "code"), suffix = c("", "_joined")) |>

Applying the corrections

# The corrections of this report, applied after checking that every listed
# questionnaire is there exactly as listed; `case_log` records each one

# Stops with the listed codes that are not found exactly once; `listed`
# holds the columns that identify the questionnaire.
expect_once <- \(listed, what) {
  found   <- listed |> left_join(count(x, pick(all_of(names(listed)))),
                                 by = names(listed))
  missing <- found$code[is.na(found$n) | found$n != 1]
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop(what, ": not found exactly once: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
         call. = FALSE)
  }
}

# Stops naming the codes, if any.
stop_if_any <- \(codes, what) {
  if (length(codes) > 0) {
    stop(what, ": ", paste(unique(codes), collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
  }
}

# the join list: every code exists, none is listed twice, none is both
# joined and a join target (no chains)
stop_if_any(setdiff(c(code_merges$code_from, code_merges$code_to), x$code),
            "Join: no questionnaire with the code")
stop_if_any(code_merges$code_from[duplicated(code_merges$code_from)],
            "Join: listed twice")
stop_if_any(intersect(code_merges$code_from, code_merges$code_to),
            "Join: joined and also a join target")

# a join must not give a person two questionnaires at one wave
clashes <- code_merges |>
  inner_join(distinct(x, code, Occasion), by = c(code_from = "code")) |>
  inner_join(distinct(x, code, Occasion), by = c(code_to = "code", "Occasion"))
stop_if_any(clashes$code_from,
            "Join: a questionnaire at the same wave as its join target")

expect_once(select(code_splits, code, Occasion, age), "Split")
expect_once(select(double_entries, code, Occasion), "Double entry")

# waves as T0 to T3; the waves of each code that a join replaces (for the log)
wave <- \(occasion) paste0("T", occasion)
joined_waves <- x |>
  filter(code %in% code_merges$code_from) |>
  summarise(wave = paste(wave(sort(unique(Occasion))), collapse = ", "),
            .by = code)

# codes that already have more than one questionnaire at a wave (copies of
# one form, see 1.5): joins and splits must not add to them, e.g. by joining
# two codes onto one
repeated_before <- x |> count(code, Occasion) |> filter(n > 1)

x <- x |>
  # one person, two codes -> one code
  left_join(select(code_merges, code = code_from, code_to), by = "code") |>
  mutate(code = coalesce(code_to, code)) |>
  select(-code_to) |>
  # two people, one code -> the second gets its own code back
  left_join(code_splits, by = c("code", "Occasion", "age")) |>
  mutate(code = coalesce(new_code, code)) |>
  select(-new_code)

repeated_after <- x |> count(code, Occasion) |> filter(n > 1)
new_repeats    <- repeated_after |>
  anti_join(repeated_before, by = c("code", "Occasion"))
stop_if_any(new_repeats$code, "Join: two questionnaires at one wave for")

# one form, entered twice -> the later entry removed
n_before <- nrow(x)
x <- x |> anti_join(double_entries, by = c("code", "Occasion"))
if (n_before - nrow(x) != nrow(double_entries)) {
  stop("Double entry: removed ", n_before - nrow(x), " entries, listed ",
       nrow(double_entries), call. = FALSE)
}

case_log <- bind_rows(
  code_merges |>
    left_join(joined_waves, by = c(code_from = "code")) |>
    transmute(correction = "codes joined", code = code_from, wave,
              change = paste("now", code_to)),
  code_splits |>
    transmute(correction = "code split", code, wave = wave(Occasion),
              change = paste("one questionnaire now", new_code)),
  double_entries |>
    transmute(correction = "double entry removed", code, wave = wave(Occasion),
              change = paste("same form as", same_form_as_code,
                             wave(same_form_as_occasion)))
)

Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
Why does a code still appear twice at one wave? The two December files of Leskovac and of Užice overlap, and a few forms were typed more than once. Kept, each copy would count the person twice at that wave. One January questionnaire of SW0429 is largely blank.
Next → Step 3, the rule: Which questionnaire stays?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
Which questionnaire stays? The largely blank questionnaire of SW0429 is dropped; of every other code and wave, the entry with the fewest missing answers stays, and of equally complete entries the first:

# One questionnaire per person and wave

x <- x |>
  # one questionnaire of SW0429 is empty apart from its code
  filter(!(code == "SW0429" & rowSums(is.na(across(everything()))) >= 70)) |>
  # copies of one form (overlapping December files of Leskovac and Užice, forms
  # typed twice) -> the entry with the fewest missing answers
  group_by(code, Occasion) |>
  slice_min(order_by = rowSums(is.na(across(everything()))),
            n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

Next → Step 4, the evidence per case: How far do the further entries agree with the first?


Step 4 · The evidence per case all questionnaires
How far do the further entries agree with the first? Each code and wave with more than one entry: the number of entries, the lowest agreement of a further entry with the first, and the number of different values in the first:

# the entries of each code and wave with more than one, numbered in the
# order of the file
copies_answers <- copies_before |>
  filter(rowSums(is.na(pick(all_of(items)))) < 70) |>   # not SW0429's
  filter(n() > 1, .by = c(code, Occasion)) |>
  mutate(entry = row_number(), .by = c(code, Occasion)) |>
  select(code, Occasion, Municipality, entry, all_of(items)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(items), names_to = "item", values_to = "answer")

repeated <- copies_answers |>
  left_join(copies_answers |>
              filter(entry == 1) |>
              select(code, Occasion, item, answer_first = answer),
            by = c("code", "Occasion", "item")) |>
  summarise(identical = round(100 * mean(answer == answer_first,
                                         na.rm = TRUE)),
            values    = n_distinct(answer_first, na.rm = TRUE),
            .by = c(code, Occasion, Municipality, entry)) |>
  summarise(entries   = n(),
            identical = min(identical[entry > 1]),
            values    = first(values),
            .by = c(code, Occasion, Municipality))

title: 1. From Questionnaires to the Analysis File
text:
1.7 Waves attended
Which waves did each person attend? Six marks per person, used in Chapter 3 to define the sample sets.

# Waves attended: six marks per person, stored with each of the person's
# questionnaires (sample sets, Chapter 3)

patterns <- x |>
  arrange(code, Occasion) |>
  summarise(pattern      = paste(sort(unique(Occasion)), collapse = "-"),
            Municipality = first(Municipality),
            .by = code) |>
  mutate(Group = if_else(Municipality %in% trained_first,
                         "Trained First", "Trained Second"))

sample_flags <- patterns |>
  mutate(
    # all four waves; at least two; January; not January only
    s1_complete       = pattern == "0-1-2-3",
    s2_no_singletons  = nchar(gsub("[^-]", "", pattern)) >= 1,
    s3_has_T0         = grepl("^0", pattern),
    # January and a wave after the own training
    s4_T0_plus_post   = case_when(
      Group == "Trained First"  ~ grepl("^0", pattern) &
                                  grepl("[1-3]", gsub("^0", "", pattern)),
      Group == "Trained Second" ~ grepl("^0", pattern) & grepl("3", pattern)
    ),
    # the waves right before and after the own training
    s5_group_baseline = case_when(
      Group == "Trained First"  ~ grepl("^0", pattern) & grepl("1", pattern),
      Group == "Trained Second" ~ grepl("2", pattern) & grepl("3", pattern)
    ),
    s6_no_T0_dropouts = pattern != "0"
  )

x <- x |>
  select(-matches("^s[1-6]_")) |>
  left_join(select(sample_flags, code, matches("^s[1-6]_")), by = "code")

1.3 Mistyped codes
Which codes were corrected before this report, and on what grounds? Codes that differ in one letter or digit, within a municipality and with the same age and sex, were set to one spelling. The corrections were found in five rounds between December 2025 and February 2026.

# Mistyped codes, corrected in five rounds (December 2025 to February 2026):
# codes that differ in one letter or digit, within a municipality and with the
# same age and sex, are set to one spelling; `mistyped` names the part of the
# code that differed (the letter, the month or the day)

# two codes that stood for more than one person -> told apart by sex and age
x <- x |>
  mutate(code = case_when(
    code == "SW0289" & sex == "M" & age == 43 ~ "SW0126",
    code == "SW0289" & sex == "F" & age == 24 ~ "SW0333",
    code == "T01"    & sex == "F" & age == 44 ~ "T62",
    code == "T01"    & sex == "F" & age == 56 ~ "SW0049",
    TRUE                                     ~ code

title: 2. Scales and Analysis Datasets
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



The two datasets of all later chapters: one row per questionnaire (df) and one row per person (df_wide). Six processing steps lead there: the items (reverse-keyed items turned around, the need-satisfaction items named by their subscales), the 23 preregistered scales, their scores and the three hypothesis composites, the design variables of the models, the codebook, and the dataset with one row per person. Each processing step is shown in the same six steps; a table at the end puts them side by side. Feeds the description of the measures in the Method section and Table 1.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)
source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)
x <- readRDS("cache/data_clean.rds")    # the analysis file (Chapter 1)

title: 2. Scales and Analysis Datasets
text:
2.2 The 23 scales
Which items make up each scale? The preregistration groups 23 scales into three hypothesis blocks: listening and togetherness (H1), cognitive complexity (H2) and well-being (H3).

# The 23 preregistered scales, their labels and hypothesis blocks; needs
# `item_names` (the 102 items, Chapter 2)

scales <- tribble(
  ~scale,                     ~label,                       ~block,
  # H1: listening and togetherness
  "ListenOther",              "Others Listen to Me",        "H1",
  "ListenSelf",               "I Listen",                   "H1",
  "Understood",               "Understood",                 "H1",
  "KamaMuta",                 "Kama Muta",                  "H1",
  "Resonance",                "Positivity Resonance",       "H1",
  "Belongingness",            "Belongingness",              "H1",
  "NoAlienation",             "No Alienation",              "H1",
  "NoIsolation",              "No Isolation",               "H1",
  # H2: cognitive complexity
  "Rogerian",                 "Rogerian Schema",            "H2",
  "ParadoxMindset",           "Paradox Mindset",            "H2",
  "IntellectualHumility",     "Intellectual Humility",      "H2",
  "ToleranceDiversity",       "Tolerance Diversity",        "H2",
  "womenAttitude",            "Women Attitude",             "H2",
  # H3: well-being
  "Flourishing",              "Flourishing",                "H3",
  "AutonomySatisfaction",     "Autonomy Satisfaction",      "H3",
  "RelatednessSatisfaction",  "Relatedness Satisfaction",   "H3",
  "CompetenceSatisfaction",   "Competence Satisfaction",    "H3",
  "AutonomyNonFrustrated",    "Autonomy Non-Frustrated",    "H3",
  "RelatednessNonFrustrated", "Relatedness Non-Frustrated", "H3",
  "CompetenceNonFrustrated",  "Competence Non-Frustrated",  "H3",
  "Empowerment",              "Empowerment",                "H3",
  "Agency",                   "Agency",                     "H3",
  "IntellectualCapital",      "Intellectual Capital",       "H3"
)

h1_scales <- scales$scale[scales$block == "H1"]
h2_scales <- scales$scale[scales$block == "H2"]
h3_scales <- scales$scale[scales$block == "H3"]

# the items of each scale: the scale name and a number, e.g. ListenOther1
scale_items <- scales$scale |>
  set_names() |>
  map(\(s) str_subset(item_names, paste0("^", s, "[0-9]+$")))

# women's attitude items 6 and 7 sit at the ceiling (T0 means above 9.7, see
# 2.3): left out of the score and of the H2 composite
ceiling_items <- c("womenAttitude6", "womenAttitude7")

# the pooled items of each hypothesis block
h1_items <- list_c(scale_items[h1_scales])
h2_items <- list_c(scale_items[h2_scales]) |> setdiff(ceiling_items)
h3_items <- list_c(scale_items[h3_scales])


scales |>
  mutate(items = lengths(scale_items))

3.3 Municipalities and trainers
How are the municipalities paired? The study randomized municipalities, not persons: each of ten trainers trained one municipality of each condition. certified is the number of participants the trainers reported as having completed the training; surveyed counts the persons who answered at least one questionnaire.

  ~Municipality, ~certified,
  "Kanjiža",     18, "Kruševac",   17, "Kula",       13, "Leskovac", 16,
  "NoviPazar",   18, "Raška",      17, "Šid",        10, "Sokobanja", 20,

  pluck("expected")

Step 2 · The problem both groups
Why can attendance not be tested like age or sex? A person contributes up to four questionnaires, so the questionnaires are not independent of each other, and a test on them overstates the evidence. title: 3. Sample
text:
3.5 Sample sets
Why sample sets? Because persons entered and left the study at different waves, the training effects are re-estimated on nested sample sets (Chapter 14). Chapter 1 marks each questionnaire with the sets its person belongs to. S7, the set without the paper forms entered twice, equals S0, because Chapter 1 already removes them from the analysis file. Chapter 4 adds two sets from the screening for careless answering (S8, S9). The eight sets of this chapter:

sample_sets <- tribble(
  ~set, ~flag,               ~definition,
  "S0", NA,                  "all questionnaires",
  "S1", "s1_complete",       "persons with all four waves",
  "S2", "s2_no_singletons",  "persons with at least two waves",
  "S3", "s3_has_T0",         "persons with a January questionnaire",
  "S4", "s4_T0_plus_post",   "January and a wave after the own training",
  "S5", "s5_group_baseline", "both waves around the own training",
  "S6", "s6_no_T0_dropouts", "not January only",
  "S7", NA,                  "without the forms entered twice (= S0)"
)

title: 4. Data quality
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Screens every questionnaire for careless answering with four indicators, combines them into two flags and turns the flags into the sample sets S8 and S9, on which Chapter 14 re-estimates the training effects. No questionnaire is removed here. The chapter also repeats the search for questionnaires entered twice on the analysis file. Every screening step goes through the same six steps, from the answers it looks at to what follows from it; a table at the end puts all steps side by side. Feeds the data-quality paragraph of the Method section and the robustness table.
source("R/packages.R")                  # all packages (Chapter 1)
source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)
df      <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")      # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds") # one row per person (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/scales.R")                    # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.2 Long strings
Did someone tick the same number again and again? A long string is a run of identical answers in the order of the questionnaire; a missing answer ends a run. Runs of agreement are plausible within a block of similar items, so the flag only counts runs that pass a reverse-keyed item, where an attentive person would switch sides.

# runs of identical answers; a missing answer ends a run
runs <- \(answer) {
  r <- rle(replace_na(answer, -1))
  tibble(length = r$lengths, value = r$values, end = cumsum(r$lengths)) |>
    mutate(start = end - length + 1) |>
    filter(value != -1)
}

# the longest run; with `through`, only runs that pass one of these item
# positions (0 if none does)
longest_run <- \(answer, through = NULL) {
  r <- runs(answer)
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(NA_integer_)
  if (!is.null(through)) {
    r <- filter(r, map2_lgl(start, end, \(s, e) any(between(through, s, e))))
  }
  max(c(0L, r$length))
}

reversed_at    <- which(item_names %in% reversed_items)
answer_rows    <- as.matrix(answers) |> asplit(1) |> map(as.vector)
ls_any         <- map_int(answer_rows, longest_run)
ls_reversed    <- map_int(answer_rows, longest_run, through = reversed_at)

Where to draw the line? Questionnaires with a run of at least k items:

tibble(run_of_at_least = c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30)) |>
  mutate(any_items        = map_int(run_of_at_least, \(k) sum(ls_any >= k,
                                                                na.rm = TRUE)),
         through_reversed = map_int(run_of_at_least, \(k) sum(ls_reversed >= k,
                                                                na.rm = TRUE)))

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.3 Agreeing with opposites
Did someone agree with an item and with its opposite? Six blocks mix positively and negatively worded items. Whoever agrees with the positive items should disagree with the negative ones, so that the mean of the positive and the mean of the negative answers add up to about 10. The inconsistency of a block is the distance of that sum from 10.

mixed_blocks <- list(
  Rogerian    = list(positive = paste0("Rogerian", 1:6),
                     negative = paste0("Rogerian", 7:9)),
  Flourishing = list(positive = paste0("Flourishing", c(1:4, 7)),
                     negative = paste0("Flourishing", 5:6)),
  Tolerance   = list(positive = paste0("ToleranceDiversity", 2:5),
                     negative = "ToleranceDiversity1"),
  Autonomy    = list(positive = paste0("AutonomySatisfaction", 1:4),
                     negative = paste0("AutonomyNonFrustrated", 1:4)),
  Relatedness = list(positive = paste0("RelatednessSatisfaction", 1:4),
                     negative = paste0("RelatednessNonFrustrated", 1:4)),
  Competence  = list(positive = paste0("CompetenceSatisfaction", 1:4),
                     negative = paste0("CompetenceNonFrustrated", 1:4))
)

# |mean of the positive + mean of the negative answers - 10|, per block
block_mean <- \(items) rowMeans(answers[items], na.rm = TRUE)
inconsistency <- mixed_blocks |>
  map(\(b) abs(block_mean(b$positive) + block_mean(b$negative) - 10)) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) if_else(is.finite(x), x, NA)))

# distance from the block's own mean, in SD of the block
inconsistency_z <- inconsistency |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) as.vector(scale(x))))

How inconsistent is a block usually? A block counts as inconsistent when it lies 2.5 SD above its own mean:

tibble(block  = names(mixed_blocks),
       M      = map_dbl(inconsistency, \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
       SD     = map_dbl(inconsistency, \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
       cutoff = M + 2.5 * SD,
       above  = map_int(inconsistency_z, \(z) sum(z >= 2.5, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.4 Even-odd consistency
Do the two halves of each scale tell the same story? Each of the 22 multi-item scales is split into its odd and its even items. Across the scales, an attentive person’s odd-half means follow their even-half means. The index is the correlation of the two within the person, stepped up to full length with the Spearman-Brown formula. It needs at least ten scales with both halves.

# the scale of an item is its name without the number; 22 of the 23 scales
# have at least two items (Understood has one)
scale_of <- str_remove(item_names, "[0-9]+$")
items_by_scale <- split(item_names, scale_of) |>
  keep(\(items) length(items) >= 2)

half_means <- \(half) items_by_scale |>
  map(\(items) rowMeans(keyed[items[half(seq_along(items))]], na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  as_tibble()
odd  <- half_means(\(i) i %% 2 == 1)
even <- half_means(\(i) i %% 2 == 0)

# the correlation of the two halves within one questionnaire
halves_r <- \(a, b) {
  ok <- is.finite(a) & is.finite(b)
  if (sum(ok) < 10 || sd(a[ok]) == 0 || sd(b[ok]) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  cor(a[ok], b[ok])
}
r_halves <- map_dbl(seq_len(nrow(keyed)),
                    \(i) halves_r(unlist(odd[i, ]), unlist(even[i, ])))
even_odd <- if_else(r_halves <= -1, -1, 2 * r_halves / (1 + r_halves))

tibble(even_odd) |> describe(even_odd)

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.5 Psychometric synonyms
Are items that go together answered together? Item pairs that correlate at .60 or more across all questionnaires are psychometric synonyms. Within a questionnaire, the answers to the first and to the second item of these pairs should correlate as well.

synonyms <- psychsyn(keyed, critval = .60, diag = TRUE, resample_na = FALSE)
synonyms |> describe(cor, numPairs)


Descriptive Statistics
----------------------
 Variable   Mean Median    SD  Range   IQR Skewness    N Missing
      cor  0.755  0.797 0.183  1.074 0.224   -1.350 1136       4
 numPairs 36.550 37.000 1.992 37.000 0.000   -9.587 1140       0

18 questionnaires fall below .22. The mirror index, psychometric antonyms, cannot be computed: no pair of items correlates at −.60 or below.

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.6 Supplementary indicators
What else stands out? Three indicators are reported but do not enter the flags. An unusual profile (Mahalanobis distance) may be careless or just unusual; low variability across all answers (intra-individual response variability, IRV) may be honest agreement with everything; and many missing items are shown as missing anyway.

# Mahalanobis distance: missing answers replaced by the item median, for
# questionnaires with at most ten missing items
n_missing <- rowSums(is.na(keyed))
imputed   <- keyed |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) replace_na(x, median(x, na.rm = TRUE))))
mahad_p   <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(keyed))
mahad_p[n_missing <= 10] <- imputed[n_missing <= 10, ] |>
  mahad(plot = FALSE) |>
  pchisq(df = ncol(keyed), lower.tail = FALSE)

irv_all <- apply(answers, 1, sd, na.rm = TRUE)

tibble(indicator = c("Mahalanobis p < .001",
                     "IRV below the 2.5th percentile",
                     "more than 25 missing items"),
       questionnaires = c(sum(mahad_p < .001, na.rm = TRUE),
                          sum(irv_all < quantile(irv_all, .025, na.rm = TRUE),
                              na.rm = TRUE),
                          sum(n_missing > 25)))

The problem · Steps 1 and 2

Step 1 · What the data look like all questionnaires
How far do two questionnaires of one person usually agree? The share of identical answers, over the items answered in both, between each person’s consecutive questionnaires:

answer_matrix <- as.matrix(answers)

dup_consecutive <- df |>
  mutate(row = row_number()) |>
  arrange(id, Occasion) |>
  mutate(previous = lag(row), .by = id) |>
  filter(!is.na(previous)) |>
  mutate(agree = map2_dbl(row, previous, \(a, b)
    mean(answer_matrix[a, ] == answer_matrix[b, ], na.rm = TRUE)))

dup_consecutive |>
  describe(agree)


Descriptive Statistics
----------------------

  --------------------------------------------------------------------
  Variable   Mean  Median     SD  Range    IQR  Skewness    N  Missing
  --------------------------------------------------------------------
  agree     0.438   0.412  0.162  0.902  0.189     0.826  689        0
  --------------------------------------------------------------------


One person, answering the same items months apart, gives the same answer to 41 % of them (median). Two entries of one paper form agree in nearly all.
Next → Step 2, the problem: Can a close match have other reasons?


Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
Can a close match have other reasons? Yes. A person who ticks the end of every scale, 0 or 10, gives nearly the same answers at every wave; two persons who both do so match each other. A form typed in twice repeats varied answers, a range of values across the scale. Varied answers make a chance match unlikely; a pair of extreme or uniform answer patterns can match by chance.
Next → Step 3, the rule: How is the search done?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
How is the search done? It compares every pair of questionnaires: pairs that agree on at least 95 % of the items both answered (and at least 80 items) are near duplicates. A pair counts as entered twice when its answers vary (at least eight different values, less than 60 % of them at 0 or 10), or when it agrees in every one of at least 100 items with at least five different values; otherwise it is an extreme pattern.

items <- as.matrix(answers)
near  <- map(seq_len(nrow(items) - 1), \(i) {
  later    <- items[(i + 1):nrow(items), , drop = FALSE]
  same     <- sweep(later, 2, items[i, ], "==")
  compared <- rowSums(!is.na(same))
  agree    <- rowSums(same, na.rm = TRUE)
  hit      <- which(compared >= 80 & agree / compared >= .95)
  tibble(i = i, j = i + hit, compared = compared[hit], agree = agree[hit])
}) |>
  list_rbind()

distinct_values <- apply(items, 1, \(a) n_distinct(a[!is.na(a)]))
extreme_percent <- 100 * rowMeans(items == 0 | items == 10, na.rm = TRUE)

near <- near |>
  mutate(id_A = df$id[i], wave_A = df$Occasion[i],
         id_B = df$id[j], wave_B = df$Occasion[j],
         distinct = pmin(distinct_values[i], distinct_values[j]),
         extreme  = round(pmax(extreme_percent[i], extreme_percent[j])),
         evidence = if_else(
           (extreme < 60 & distinct >= 8) |
             (agree == compared & compared >= 100 & distinct >= 5),
           "entered twice", "extreme pattern")) |>
  select(id_A, wave_A, id_B, wave_B, compared, agree, distinct, extreme,
         evidence)

SW0081 and SW0090 belong to the same municipality and the same trainer; one is ten years older than the other. Both answer only with 0 and 10; as analysed, they give 10 to more than nine in ten items and deviate from it at the same items. In January and in March they agree in all 102 items, and from January to March both change the same 4 answers (Paradox Mindset 3, Autonomy Non-Frustrated 1 and 2, Autonomy Satisfaction 3); only in September do they part (89 % agreement).
Answering this much alike independently is unlikely. title: 7. Measurement invariance over time and groups
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Tests for each of the 22 latent constructs whether the questionnaire measures it the same way at all four waves and in both groups. The two groups were trained at different times, so each group is first examined on its own: do its loadings and intercepts stay the same over the four waves? Then the two groups are compared: are their loadings and intercepts the same? Every model goes through the same checks, in the order of the textbooks: did the estimation converge, is its solution possible, how well does it fit, where does it strain. A model whose solution is not possible stops; the mildest change that makes it possible carries the steps on, and a construct for which there is none goes no further. Every construct goes through the same twelve steps and ends with its status and the model that goes on to the difference-in-differences of Chapter 11. Feeds the measurement-invariance paragraph of the Results and the invariance table of the supplement.

source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)
df      <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")      # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds") # one row per person (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/scales.R")                    # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)
source("R/measurement.R")               # models of the constructs (Chapter 6)
source("R/longitudinal_models.R")       # waves, at(), wave_pairs
source("R/longitudinal_effects.R")      # the models of this chapter (7.2)

title: 11. Latent difference-in-differences
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Estimates the training effects on the latent means of every construct that Chapter 7 carries on: how much more the experimental group changes than the control group while it trains (January to March), and the mirrored effect when the control group trains (September to December). Each construct starts from its final model of Chapter 7, with its measurement held equal over the waves and the groups, and adds age and sex as covariates and every contrast as a parameter. Every model goes through the checks of Chapter 7; what the covariates add is tested like a step of Chapter 7, and a construct whose covariates fail goes on without them. Every construct goes through the same nine steps and ends with the effects that the synthesis of Chapter 20 reads. Feeds the latent results of Hypotheses 1 to 3, the wait-list replication, the latent effect sizes and the sensitivity tables of the supplement.

title: 9. Means and Δd
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Describes the scale scores by condition and wave and measures the change of each group in standard deviations (repeated-measures d). The difference between the groups, Δd, is the descriptive counterpart of the difference-in-differences: while the experimental group trains (T0 to T1) and while the control group trains (T2 to T3). Each of the 23 scales and the three hypothesis composites goes through the same steps: its means by condition and wave, Δd in four windows with its interval, Δd with the standard deviation of all questionnaires before the window, and the p corrected for testing many scales. A dropout analysis asks whether the later gains come from who stays in the study, and a table and a figure at the end set all outcomes side by side. Feeds the table and figures of means and effect sizes of the Results; Chapter 14 repeats the Δd on the sample sets S0 to S9.

title: 10. Multilevel models
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



The preregistered test of the training effects, outcome by outcome: one multilevel model per outcome with the interaction of wave and condition, questionnaires nested in persons nested in municipalities, and the same model with the trainers as a further level. Two further models replicate the effect when the control group trains, random slopes ask whether the change differs between trainers, municipalities and persons, also within each condition, and equivalence tests check the claims that the groups do not differ at baseline and after both trainings. Each of the 23 scales and the three hypothesis composites goes through the same eight steps. One-sided tests and a correction for testing many outcomes then show how much the counts of significant effects depend on these choices, and a table at the end puts all outcomes side by side. Feeds the preregistered results of Hypotheses 1 to 3.

title: 13. Movers
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Looks at single persons instead of means: who improved, stayed the same or declined between two waves, under three criteria of change. For Tolerance Diversity and Women Attitude, whose means barely moved, it asks whether the trained group improved more often in its own training window. Both scales go through the same seven steps: the score and its reliability, the bands that separate change from no change, the movers while the experimental group trains, the movers from baseline, the rates of improvement in each group’s own training window, the verdict, and what follows. A table at the end puts both scales side by side. Exploratory; feeds a supplementary paragraph of the paper.

title: 14. Robustness across sample sets
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Repeats the training effects on the sample sets S0 to S9, effect by effect: the repeated-measures Δd of Chapter 9 for each of the 23 scales and the three hypothesis composites, once for each way of choosing persons and questionnaires, also with the standard deviation of all questionnaires before the window, and for the composites the preregistered multilevel models of Chapter 10. Every outcome goes through the same five steps: Δd in every set, another standard deviation, the multilevel model in every set, the verdict, and what follows. An effect that holds across the sets does not depend on who answered when or on careless answering; the latent effects on the same sets are Step 7 of each construct in Chapter 11. A table at the end puts all effects side by side. Feeds the robustness table of the supplement.

title: 12. Serial mediation
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Tests the preregistered pathway of the training: training → listening and togetherness (H1) → cognitive complexity (H2) → well-being (H3), in four windows between two waves. Every window goes through the same seven steps: its model, the path diagram, the paths, the indirect effects with bootstrap confidence intervals, the check with complete cases and cluster-robust standard errors, and a model with latent blocks (structural after measurement) that asks whether the effects hold when measurement error is modelled. A section at the end puts the four windows side by side. Feeds the mediation results of the paper (Chapter 20) and the comparison with the post hoc structure (Chapter 19).

title: 5. Reliability and baseline correlations
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



How consistently the items of each scale measure at each wave (Cronbach’s α, McDonald’s ω), and how each scale correlates with the other 22 in January (T0). Each of the 23 scales goes through the same four steps: its items, α and ω per wave, its correlations with the other scales, and what follows from them. The three hypothesis composites go through the same steps; five composites that cut across the blocks (need satisfaction and need non-frustration, the negatively and the positively worded items, all items) go through the first two. The chapter ends with all correlations side by side and a table across all scales and composites. Feeds the reliabilities of Table 1 and the description of the measures.

title: 15. Item pruning
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



The preregistration allowed a psychometric study that would “discard unreliable and redundant items to create more parsimonious measures”. Part D carries it out after the fact, on the questionnaires answered before any training (T0). This chapter takes items out of the pool by three rules before any network is estimated: answers at the ceiling, negative wording, and the block on attitudes toward women. Each rule goes through the same five steps, from the items it looks at to what its decision means for the scales; on the way, the chapter shows that the negatively worded items hardly respond to the training. A table at the end follows every scale through the three rules. Feeds the pruning step of the psychometric supplement; Chapters 16 to 18 build on the remaining pool.

source("R/settings.R")                  # waves, conditions, folders (Chapter 1)

df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds") # one row per person (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/scales.R")                    # the 23 scales (Chapter 2)

title: 15. Item pruning
text:
15.3 Negative wording
Do the negatively worded items respond to the training? Negatively worded items tend to form communities of their own in a network, defined by the direction of the wording rather than by its content, and they invite more answering errors. If they also carried the training effect, dropping them would cost signal. The test is the first training window: how much does each item move from T0 to T1 in the experimental group, beyond the change in the control group?
The measure here is a difference-in-differences d per item: the change of each group’s mean from T0 to T1, divided by the standard deviation at T0 pooled over both groups, experimental minus control. Unlike the Δd of Chapter 9, the means use every questionnaire of a group and wave, not only persons who answered at both waves. The negatively worded items enter reverse-keyed (Chapter 2), so a positive d always means a move toward the desired pole.

item_effects <- item_did(df) |>
  mutate(wording = if_else(item %in% negative_items, "negative",
                           "positive"))

item_effects |>

            median_d   = median(d_did),
            mean_abs_d = mean(abs(d_did)),
            mean_d_E   = mean(d_E),
            .by = wording) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

title: 15. Item pruning
text:
15.4 The women’s attitude block
Why does the whole block go? Beyond the two items at the ceiling, the other seven items of the block sit close to it as well, so the block as a whole gives a network little variance to work with. title: 16. Exploratory graph analysis
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Exploratory graph analysis (EGA) estimates a network of the items and finds the communities of items that hang together. Starting from the pool of Chapter 15, three analyses follow one another: the first keeps the items whose community holds across bootstrap samples, the second describes the hierarchical structure of these items at each wave, and the third bootstraps that structure. Each analysis goes through the same six steps, from the items it starts with to where its result goes next; a table at the end follows every scale through the three analyses. Feeds the item-selection and structure steps of the psychometric supplement; Chapter 17 prunes the stable items further.

title: 17. Redundancy and item response theory
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Two rules prune the stable items of Chapter 16 further. An item response model per community flags items that hardly separate persons with low from persons with high standing on their community; the same models at each of the four waves show whether discriminations, thresholds and test information hold over time. A redundancy analysis finds pairs of items so close that one of them adds nothing. Each of the three analyses goes through the same six steps, from the items and answers it starts with to where its result goes next; a table at the end follows every community to the items it keeps. Feeds the redundancy and discrimination step of the psychometric supplement; Chapter 18 builds the final structure on the items that remain.

title: 18. Final structure
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



The structure of the final item pool, in seven analyses that follow one another: the hierarchical structure of the items at each wave and its bootstrap, the composite score of each community, how the composites group into factors at T0 and at each wave, the information of every item, and the reliability of every composite. title: 18. Final structure
text:
18.5 The master table
How good is each item? For the final structure: each item’s factor, composite, GRM discrimination a, Fisher information I(θ) at three trait levels (θ = −2, 0, +2, about two standard deviations below the mean, the mean, two above), and its correlation with the mean of the other items of its composite. The GRMs are fitted per composite with at least three items, on the T0 questionnaires that answer all its items.

factors <- composites |>
  distinct(higher, composite) |>
  mutate(factor = factor_name(composite), .by = higher)

grm <- composites |>
  filter(n() >= 3, .by = composite) |>
  summarise(fit = list(grm_fit(items_T0[item])), .by = composite) |>
  mutate(reliability = map_dbl(fit, marginal_rxx),
         a           = map(fit, discrimination),
         information = map(fit, item_information))

master <- composites |>
  arrange(higher, lower) |>
  left_join(select(factors, composite, factor), by = "composite") |>
  mutate(item_rest = item_rest(items_T0[item]), .by = composite) |>
  left_join(grm |> select(a) |> unnest(a), by = "item") |>
  left_join(grm |> select(information) |> unnest(information) |>
              pivot_wider(names_from = theta, values_from = information,
                          names_prefix = "I_"),
            by = "item") |>
  select(factor, composite, item, a, `I_-2`, I_0, I_2, item_rest)

title: 19. Training effects on the new structure
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Re-estimates the training effects on the structure found in the data (Chapter 18): two factors, Engagement and Well-being and agency, their ten communities, and the single item on life satisfaction. The questions are those of Part C: does the trained group gain more in each training window, and does the training reach well-being through engagement? Each factor and the single item go through the same six steps: the score, its means by condition and wave, Δd in the two training windows, the preregistered multilevel model, whether the factor is measured the same way at all four waves (as a latent difference-in-differences would need), and what follows. The pathway from the training through Engagement to Well-being and agency is then estimated in the four windows of Chapter 12, each in five steps. A section at the end puts all results side by side. Exploratory: the structure was derived from the same questionnaires (at T0), so these results describe this sample and need replication. Feeds the post hoc section of the paper (Chapter 20).

title: 20. Synthesis
section: 20.1 Three estimates of the training effect
text:
20.1 Three estimates of the training effect
Where do the methods agree? While the experimental group trains (T0 to T1), the effect of each scale in three estimates: the descriptive Δd (Chapter 9), the preregistered multilevel interaction at T1 (Chapter 10) and the latent difference-in-differences (Chapter 11, only where Chapter 7 finds the measurement the same over the waves and in both groups). methods counts the estimates that are significant (p < .05) in favour of the training.

significant_up <- \(estimate, p) !is.na(p) & p < .05 & estimate > 0

agreement <- scales |>
  select(outcome = scale, label, block) |>
  left_join(means$effects |>
              filter(pre == "T0", post == "T1") |>
              select(outcome, delta_d, p_delta_d = p),
            by = "outcome") |>
  left_join(multilevel$interactions |>
              filter(wave == "T1") |>
              select(outcome, b_mlm = b, p_mlm = p),
            by = "outcome") |>
  left_join(smm$training_effects |>
              select(outcome = construct, did_latent = DiD_T01_est,
                     p_latent = DiD_T01_pvalue),
            by = "outcome") |>
  mutate(methods = significant_up(delta_d, p_delta_d) +
           significant_up(b_mlm, p_mlm) +
           significant_up(did_latent, p_latent))

  select(block, label, delta_d, b_mlm, did_latent, methods) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>

20.2 The wait-list replication
Does the effect return when the control group trains? The mirrored estimates for T2 to T3 (negative: the control group gains more):

title: 20. Synthesis
text:
20.4 Where the results are fragile
What limits these conclusions?

limits <- tibble(
  limit = c("latent models without the covariates (Chapter 11)",
            "constructs that stop in Chapter 7",
            "constructs with partial invariance (Chapter 7)",
            "sample sets in which H2 misses significance (Chapter 14)",
            "mover contrasts significant (Chapter 13)",
            "scales with a Δd for the training after BH correction (Chapter 9)",
            "latent training effects after BH correction (Chapter 11)"),
  n = c(sum(!smm$models$covariates),
        sum(!invariance$adopted$chapter_11),
        sum(lengths(invariance$adopted$freed) > 0),
        robustness$delta_d |>
          filter(outcome == "H2_CognitiveComplexity", pre == "T0",
                 post == "T1", p >= .05) |> nrow(),
        movers$window_rates |> distinct(score, pre, p) |>
          filter(p < .05) |> nrow(),
        means$corrected |>
          filter(pre == "T0", post == "T1", family == "scales",
                 p_BH < .05, delta_d > 0) |> nrow(),
        smm$adjusted |>
          filter(DiD_T01_p_BH < .05, DiD_T01_est > 0) |> nrow())

Two constructs stop in Chapter 7, I Listen and Women Attitude: their measurement does not stay the same in one group, so their latent means are not compared. Every latent model of the others is possible, several only after the stop rule of Chapter 7 set estimates at 0 or held autocorrelations equal; under the stricter cutoffs for small samples, more constructs would stop at one step or more (Chapter 7.6). 5 constructs are measured alike only in part, with one item freed in one group, among them Autonomy Satisfaction, which show the effect in all three estimates; their latent effects rest on the items that are measured alike. Kama Muta is compared without the covariates; with them, its effects are nearly the same (Chapter 11). By Cohen’s labels the latent effects are small (Chapter 11.7).
Correcting for testing 23 scales at once (Benjamini-Hochberg) leaves 1 scale with a Δd for the training and 5 of the 7 latent training effects; tested one-sided, as the hypotheses are directional, all three composites show the multilevel effect at T1. With the standard deviation of all questionnaires before the window, the replication while the control group trains shrinks from 9 to 5 scales (Chapter 9.9). Other choices leave the picture in place: a trainer level adds nothing to the multilevel models (Chapter 10.8), and dropout does not explain the late gains in well-being (Chapter 9.8). Δd and the latent models leave out that persons are clustered in municipalities; the multilevel models, which take the municipalities into account, and the cluster-robust mediation give the same picture.
The effect on Cognitive Complexity holds in eight of nine sample sets and misses significance only among the 127 persons with all four waves. At the level of single persons, no scale separates the groups significantly (Chapter 13). The post hoc structure was found in the same data and partly selected for responsiveness to the training, and neither of its two factors is scalar invariant over the waves (Chapter 19.3), so its effects rest on manifest scores and need a new sample.

title: 8. Simultaneous block models
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Chapters 6 and 7 model each construct alone. Here all constructs of one hypothesis block enter one factor model, which answers two questions a single construct cannot: are the constructs of a block empirically distinct (discriminant validity), and does the block as a whole stay invariant over time? Every block goes through the same seven steps: its model and the checks of its solution at each wave, then its latent correlations and the discriminant validity of its constructs, then its invariance over adjacent waves and over the whole year. As in Chapter 7, the checks come first, and a model whose solution is not possible, or that does not fit, stops: its estimates are not read. Two tables at the end put the three blocks side by side. Feeds the discriminant-validity paragraph and the block-level invariance table of the supplement.

title: 9. Means and Δd
text:
9.8 Dropout
Why look at dropout? The later windows rest on ever fewer persons (Section 9.3), and in the experimental group well-being keeps rising after the training: its d grows from 0.16 (T0 to T1) to 0.36 (T0 to T3). Both could come from who stays in the study rather than from change within the same persons. Four questions, asked of the three composites, tell the two apart.
Who stays after T1? Of the persons with a January questionnaire, those who answered again in September or December stay; the others leave after T1 (or after T0):

# persons with a questionnaire in September or December

  filter(Occasion %in% c("T2", "T3")) |>
  distinct(id) |>
  mutate(after_T1 = "stays")

baseline <- df |>
  filter(Occasion == "T0") |>
  left_join(stayers, by = "id") |>
  mutate(after_T1 = factor(coalesce(after_T1, "leaves"),

title: 17. Redundancy and item response theory
text:
17.4 The models at each wave
Does every item separate low from high at every wave? The GRMs of 17.3 once more at each wave, on the questionnaires of that wave that answer every stable item. Each community’s marginal reliability and its smallest discrimination:

modelled <- communities |> filter(n() >= 3, .by = community)

wave_grm <- tibble(wave = levels(df$Occasion)) |>
  mutate(answers = map(wave, \(w)
    items_at(df, w, communities$item) |> drop_na())) |>
  expand_grid(community = unique(modelled$community)) |>
  mutate(items       = map2(answers, community, \(a, c)
           a[modelled$item[modelled$community == c]]),

         persons     = map_int(items, nrow),
         converged   = map_lgl(fit, \(f) extract.mirt(f, "converged")),

NoteAbout this chapter



What the team asked for in its e-mails about the analyses and about this documentation, from June 2025 to November 2026, and where each request stands now. The list was compiled from the e-mails and checked against the chapters of this documentation. Organisational matters and the wording of the paper are not part of it; requests about the paper are only summarised at the end. Computes nothing.

title: 24. Requests and their status
text:
24.1 How the list was made
Where do the requests come from? The team discussed the analyses in 52 e-mail threads between June 2025 and November 2026. Every request in them was noted, 269 in all: questions, proposals, corrections and the tasks of the work plans.
Which requests are left out? Of these, 56 were organisational, about travel, funding, meetings and submissions; they are left out. Another 49 concern the paper rather than this documentation, such as the text of its sections, its figures or the literature; they are summarised in 24.14. Each of the other 164 requests was checked against the chapters: is the analysis there, in which section, and in the form that was asked for?
How is a request written here? In one plain sentence, in the words of this documentation rather than those of the e-mail. Requests that ask for the same thing share a row. The column Where names the section, for example 9.3 for Chapter 9, Section 3; a dash marks a request that concerns the whole documentation or that no section answers.

title: 24. Requests and their status
text:
24.13 Decisions that remain open
Which choices are still to be made? For six questions the documentation shows the alternatives side by side, so that the team can decide with the results in view:

Cutoffs for invariance. Whether the conventional cutoffs or the stricter ones for small samples decide; under the stricter ones, 14 constructs would stop at one step or more (Chapter 7.6).
Multiple testing and one-sided tests. Whether the results are corrected for testing many scales at once, and whether they are tested one-sided, as the directional hypotheses would allow (Chapters 9.3, 10.7 and 11.3).
The standard deviation of Δd. Whether Δd is standardized by the persons who answered at both waves of a window or by all questionnaires before it; the choice matters mainly for the replication while the control group trains (Chapter 9.9).
Trainers in the multilevel models. Whether the models include the trainers as a level, as preregistered, although the trainers add almost nothing and change no verdict (Chapter 10.8).
The covariate step of the latent models. Whether what the covariates add is tested against a model in which age and sex act on every item directly (nested, as now), or by comparing the fit with the model of Chapter 7, which holds fewer variables; under the second, five constructs would stop at that step (Chapter 11.1, Step 3).
Post hoc factors. How to report the effects on the two post hoc factors, which are not measured alike at all four waves, so that their effects rest on manifest scores only (Chapter 19.3).

title: 24. Requests and their status
text:
24.14 Requests about the paper
What did the team ask about the paper? Of the 213 requests, 49 concern the paper or the work on it rather than this documentation. Most are about its text, from the introduction to the discussion and the choice of journal (19), its figures and tables, among them the table of deviations from the preregistration (8), and the literature (6); seven concern the qualitative part of the study, which this documentation does not cover, and nine how tasks and files were shared within the team. Where they need numbers, these come from the chapters that Chapter 0 assigns to each part of the paper.

title: 6. Measurement models per wave
text:
6.1 How each construct is examined
Why both groups together at T0, and each group on its own later? In January nobody had been trained, and both groups answer alike: the models are settled on the January questionnaires of both groups together, and each group is checked on its own. From March on, the groups differ by their training, at different times; from there on every model is fitted in each group separately.
What happens to each construct? The same nine steps, in the same order:

The items. Which questions measure the construct, in their wording, and which of them were asked the other way round (reverse-keyed).
The answers. How the answers spread over the scale from 0 to 10 in January (T0): mean, spread, skew, and how many answered 10. Answers that pile up at the top of the scale are the reason why every model below uses robust maximum likelihood (MLR).
How the items hang together. The correlations between the items (from three items on as a heat map), how strongly each item goes with the rest (its discrimination), and Cronbach’s α without each item.
One factor at T0. A confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) with one factor on all items, in the January questionnaires of both groups: its path diagram with the fit, and its standardized loadings.
Where it strains. Items that load weakly (below .40) and pairs of items that share more than the factor explains (modification indices, MI, of 10 and more). The fit counts as good from a robust CFI of .95 and an SRMR below .08; the RMSEA is reported but overstates misfit when a model has few degrees of freedom (Kenny et al., 2015).
The decision. Whether the model is kept as it is or revised, one change at a time, each with its reason, and the fit before and after.
The decision in both groups. The same model with all items, in each group’s January questionnaires: whether the same items load weakly and the same pairs strain, and whether the final model fits in each group.
The four waves, in each group. The final model, fitted unchanged at T0, T1, T2 and T3, first in the control and then in the experimental group: whether its solution is possible, its fit, its reliability, and the loading of every item at every wave. A wave falls short with a CFI below .95 or an RMSEA above .15; where the CFI falls short, the modification indices of the weakest wave show where the model strains. Single waves hold 69 to 180 questionnaires per group and judge a model only roughly; whether the loadings and intercepts stay the same over time is tested in Chapter 7, with all four waves at once.
What follows. Which items carry the construct into the later chapters, and what the invariance tests of Chapter 7 find for it.

title: 6. Measurement models per wave
text:
6.2 Data and tools
Which data? The January questionnaires of both groups and of each group for steps 1 to 7, and each group’s four waves, one data set each, for step 8:

t0                 <- filter(df, Occasion == "T0")
t0_groups          <- split(t0, t0$condition)
control_waves      <- df |> filter(condition == "Control") |>
  split(~ Occasion)
experimental_waves <- df |> filter(condition == "Experimental") |>
  split(~ Occasion)
invariance         <- readRDS("cache/invariance.rds")

What does Chapter 7 find? The summary of Step 9 ends with the outcome of the invariance tests of Chapter 7; for a construct that enters Chapter 11, it is written from the status Chapter 7 saved:

# the outcome of Chapter 7 for a construct that enters Chapter 11: the
# adjustments of the stop rule and the items freed, as a sentence
ch7_sentence <- \(status) {
  freed <- status$freed[[1]]
  how <- c(
    if (str_detect(status$status, "\\(A\\)"))
      "with estimates outside their range set at 0 (adjustment A)",
    if (str_detect(status$status, "\\(B\\)"))
      "with one autocorrelation per item over the waves (adjustment B)",
    if (length(freed) > 0)
      str_c("except for item ", unique(str_extract(freed, "[0-9]+(?= )")),
            " in the ", str_to_lower(unique(str_extract(freed, "^[A-Za-z]+"))),
            " group (partial invariance)"))
  str_c("the same over the four waves and in both groups",
        if (length(how) > 0) str_c(", ", str_flatten(how, ", ")), ".")
}

Which tools? The analysis of each step is written out for every construct. Only the figures and two summary tables use small functions, defined once here:

AnswersCorrelationsPath diagramFit and reliabilityLoadings over the wavesItem wording



# the share of each answer (0 to 10), one panel per item
plot_answers <- \(items) {
  items |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "item", values_to = "answer") |>
    filter(!is.na(answer)) |>
    count(item, answer) |>
    mutate(share = n / sum(n), .by = item) |>
    mutate(item = factor(item, levels = names(items))) |>
    ggplot(aes(answer, share)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6", width = .8) +
    facet_wrap(~ item, ncol = 4) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 5, 10)) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
    labs(x = "answer as scored (0 to 10)", y = "share of the answers") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}




# the item correlations as a lower triangle: blue positive, red negative,
# grey near zero
plot_correlations <- \(items) {
  r <- cor(items, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  r[upper.tri(r, diag = TRUE)] <- NA
  as_tibble(r, rownames = "row") |>
    pivot_longer(-row, names_to = "column", values_to = "r") |>
    filter(!is.na(r)) |>
    mutate(row    = factor(row, levels = rev(names(items))),
           column = factor(column, levels = names(items))) |>
    ggplot(aes(column, row, fill = r)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_text(aes(label = apa(r)), size = 3.4) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#e34948", mid = "#f0efec", high = "#2a78d6",
                         limits = c(-1, 1)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
          axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
}




# the fit beside the diagram, and its title above
semgraphic_text <- \(fit, title = "") {
  values <- fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq.scaled", "df.scaled", "pvalue.scaled",
                               "cfi.robust", "tli.robust", "rmsea.robust",
                               "srmr"))
  labels <- c("ChiSq", "df", "p", "CFI", "TLI", "RMSEA", "SRMR")
  text(1.1, -1, labels = str_c(labels, " = ", round(values, 3),
                               collapse = "\n"),
       pos = 4, cex = .75)
  text(0, 1.4, labels = title, cex = 1)
}

# the model as a path diagram: standardized estimates, stars for their
# significance
cfaPlot <- \(fit, title) {
  semPaths(fit, whatLabels = "std", style = "mx", layout = "tree",
           edge.color = "black", intercepts = FALSE, asize = 2.5,
           sizeMan = 6.5, sizeLat = 7, edge.label.cex = .8,
           edge.label.position = .8, mar = c(3, 2, 5, 9),
           DoNotPlot = TRUE) |>
    mark_sig(fit) |>
    plot()
  semgraphic_text(fit, title)
}




# the fit of a model in one row, and whether its solution is possible
# (lavaan's check for negative variances and covariances that are not
# positive definite)
fit_table <- \(fit) {
  fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq.scaled", "df", "pvalue.scaled", "cfi.robust",
                     "tli.robust", "rmsea.robust", "srmr")) |>
    as.list() |>
    as_tibble() |>
    set_names(c("ChiSq", "df", "p", "CFI", "TLI", "RMSEA", "SRMR")) |>
    mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 3)),
           ChiSq = round(ChiSq, 2)) |>
    mutate(admissible = suppressWarnings(lavInspect(fit, "post.check")),
           .before = 1)
}

# α, ω and the average variance extracted (AVE) of a model, with its
# lowest and highest standardized loading
reliability_check <- \(fit) {
  loadings <- standardizedSolution(fit) |> filter(op == "=~")
  tibble(alpha    = compRelSEM(fit, tau.eq = TRUE),
         omega    = compRelSEM(fit),
         AVE      = AVE(fit),
         min_load = min(loadings$est.std),
         max_load = max(loadings$est.std)) |>
    mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(as.numeric(x), 3)))
}




# the standardized loading of each item at each wave
wave_colours <- c(T0 = "#2a78d6", T1 = "#eb6834", T2 = "#1baf7a",
                  T3 = "#eda100")
plot_loadings_waves <- \(fits) {
  fits |>
    map(\(fit) standardizedSolution(fit) |> filter(op == "=~")) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "wave") |>
    ggplot(aes(wave, est.std, group = rhs)) +
    geom_line(colour = "grey70", linewidth = .6) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = wave), size = 2.6) +
    geom_text(data = \(d) filter(d, wave == "T3"), aes(label = rhs),
              hjust = -.15, size = 3.3) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = wave_colours, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(.3, 1.6))) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "standardized loading") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

Which constructs? The eight scales of the first hypothesis. Seven of them have two or more items and go through all eight steps; one of them, Positivity Resonance, needs a revision at T0. Understood has a single item.

Step 4 · One factor at T0
What does the model look like? Two items cannot identify a factor with free loadings, so both loadings are held equal (tau-equivalent) and the factor variance is set to 1:

  cfa(model = "
        ListenOther =~ NA*ListenOther1 + L*ListenOther1 + L*ListenOther2
        ListenOther ~~ 1*ListenOther

      data = _, estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml.x")

Step 9 · What follows

Where does the construct go from here? Both items form its score (Chapter 2) and its latent factor in Chapters 7, 8 and 11.
