# Item pruning (Chapter 15): which items leave the pool before the network
# analyses, and how strongly each item moves while the experimental group
# trains. Needs `item_names` (the 102 items, Chapter 2).

# the 22 negatively worded items, reverse-keyed in Chapter 2
negative_items <- c("NoAlienation1", "NoAlienation2",
                    "NoIsolation1", "NoIsolation2",
                    "Flourishing5", "Flourishing6", paste0("Rogerian", 7:9),
                    "ToleranceDiversity1",
                    str_subset(item_names, "NonFrustrated"))

# items with a T0 mean above the cutoff: hardly any room left to vary
items_at_ceiling <- \(data, cutoff = 9.7) {
  data |>
    filter(Occasion == "T0") |>
    summarise(across(all_of(item_names), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "item", values_to = "mean") |>
    filter(mean > cutoff) |>
    pull(item)
}

# why an item leaves the pool (NA: it stays); the first reason that applies
pruning_reasons <- \(data) {
  at_ceiling <- items_at_ceiling(data)
  tibble(item = item_names) |>
    mutate(reason = case_when(
      item %in% at_ceiling              ~ "ceiling",
      item %in% negative_items          ~ "negative wording",
      str_starts(item, "womenAttitude") ~ "women's attitude block",
      .default = NA
    ))
}

# the items that stay, in the order of the questionnaire
structure_pool <- \(data) {
  pruning_reasons(data) |>
    filter(is.na(reason)) |>
    pull(item)
}

# change from T0 to T1 in each group, over the SD of both groups at T0;
# d_did is the difference of the two. Cell means use every questionnaire
# of a group and wave, not only persons who answered at both waves.
item_did <- \(data) {
  data |>
    filter(Occasion %in% c("T0", "T1")) |>
    pivot_longer(all_of(item_names), names_to = "item") |>
    summarise(m = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
              v = var(value, na.rm = TRUE),
              n = sum(!is.na(value)),
              .by = c(item, condition, Occasion)) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = c(condition, Occasion),
                values_from = c(m, v, n)) |>
    mutate(sd_T0 = sqrt(((n_Experimental_T0 - 1) * v_Experimental_T0 +
                           (n_Control_T0 - 1) * v_Control_T0) /
                          (n_Experimental_T0 + n_Control_T0 - 2)),
           d_E   = (m_Experimental_T1 - m_Experimental_T0) / sd_T0,
           d_C   = (m_Control_T1 - m_Control_T0) / sd_T0,
           d_did = d_E - d_C) |>
    select(item, sd_T0, d_E, d_C, d_did)
}




The three rules remove 31 items and leave 71. The pool loses 6 scales entirely: No Alienation, No Isolation, Women Attitude, Autonomy Non-Frustrated, Relatedness Non-Frustrated, and Competence Non-Frustrated. The remaining 17 scales enter the network analyses of Chapter 16 with all their positively worded items.
Chapter 16 asks which of the 71 items keep their place in a network of all items.

title: 16. Exploratory graph analysis
section: 16.1 How each network analysis is examined
text:
16.1 How each network analysis is examined
How does EGA find communities? The graphical lasso turns the correlations of the items into a network of partial correlations: two items are linked only if they share something that the other items do not explain, and weak links are set to zero. A community detection algorithm then groups items that are densely linked with each other (Golino & Epskamp, 2017). The bootstrap repeats this on 500 samples drawn from a normal distribution with the observed correlations. An item’s stability is the share of samples in which it lands in the same community as in the observed data (Christensen & Golino, 2021). The hierarchical version (hierEGA) adds a second level: it scores the persons on each community of items (lower order) and runs EGA on these scores, which yields factors of communities (higher order).
What happens in each analysis? The same six steps, in the same order and in three parts: the analysis, its result, and what follows. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph P0["the analysis"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>the starting point"]
    S1 --> S2["<b>Step 2</b><br>the method and<br>the criterion"]
    S2 --> S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>the estimation"]
  end
  subgraph P1["the result"]
    direction LR
    S4{{"<b>Step 4</b><br>the result"}}
    S4 --> S5["<b>Step 5</b><br>the scales<br>behind it"]
  end
  V["<b>Step 6</b><br>what follows"]
  P0 --> P1
  P1 --> V

  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f

The six steps in detail:
The analysis:

The starting point. Which items enter, from which questionnaires, and in which order: the community algorithms and the bootstrap draws depend on the order of the items.
The method and the criterion. How the analysis estimates the network and its communities, and by which criterion it judges them. An item is stable when it lands in the same community as in the observed data in at least 60 % of the bootstrap samples. A community or a factor is structurally consistent when it reappears with exactly the same items in at least 75 % of the samples. Two partitions of the same items are compared by the share of item pairs they treat alike, both together or both apart (the Rand index), which is 1 when they are the same; the total entropy fit index (TEFI) compares solutions on the same items, lower is better.
The estimation. The code. The bootstraps take a few minutes each and run in a script of their own, which also carries the steps of Chapters 17 and 18; this chapter reads their results. The hierarchical solutions at each wave are estimated here.

The result:

The result. What the analysis finds: items, communities and factors, with a figure where it shows something.
The scales behind it. What the result means for the scales the items come from.

What follows:

What follows. Where the result goes next.

title: 16. Exploratory graph analysis
text:
16.2 Data and tools
Which data? The T0 questionnaires for the two bootstraps, all four waves, one data set each, for the hierarchical solutions, and the results of the bootstraps:

t0      <- filter(df, Occasion == "T0")
list_df <- split(df, df$Occasion)
ega     <- readRDS("cache/structure_ega.rds")    # the two bootstraps

The script stores, for the first bootstrap, the pool it starts from (pool), each of its passes (passes), the stability of the items of the last pass (stability) and the stable items in the order of their community (stable); for the bootstrap of the hierarchical solution, the stability of every item at both levels (hier_items) and the structural consistency of the communities (hier_lower) and of the factors (hier_higher).
Which tools? What runs in this chapter is written out below. The script of the bootstraps, the network functions it calls, and one small function for the figures of the bootstrap results are shown once here:

Pipeline scriptNetwork functionsBootstrap shares



# Post hoc psychometrics: the bootstraps and the chain of item selections
# of Chapters 16 to 18. The T0 questionnaires calibrate every step; the
# composites are bootstrapped again at each wave.
# Run from swt-website/ after Chapter 2:  Rscript scripts/structure_pipeline.R

source("R/packages.R")
source("R/settings.R")
df <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")           # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/structure_pool.R")            # item pruning (Chapter 15)
source("R/structure_ega.R")             # network analyses (Chapter 16)
source("R/structure_irt.R")             # redundancy and IRT (Chapter 17)
source("R/structure_composites.R")      # composites (Chapter 18)

# Chapter 16: bootstrap until every item is stable, then bootstrap the
# hierarchical solution of the stable items. The items are ordered by
# community and stability; louvain and the bootstrap draws depend on the
# order of the items.
pool      <- structure_pool(df)
converged <- converge_ega(items_at(df, "T0", pool))
stable    <- converged$stability |>
  arrange(community, desc(stability)) |>
  pull(item)
boot_hier <- boot_hier_ega(items_at(df, "T0", stable))

saveRDS(list(pool        = pool,
             passes      = converged$passes,
             stability   = converged$stability,
             stable      = stable,
             hier_items  = hier_item_stability(boot_hier),
             hier_lower  = structural_consistency(boot_hier, "lower_order"),
             hier_higher = structural_consistency(boot_hier, "higher_order")),
        "cache/structure_ega.rds")

# Chapter 17: GRM per community and UVA on the persons who answered all
# stable items; the communities come from the bootstrap above
communities <- hier_item_stability(boot_hier) |>
  select(item, community = lower, stability = stability_lower)
calibration <- items_at(df, "T0", communities$item) |> drop_na()
pruned      <- community_discrimination(calibration, communities) |>
  prune_items(redundant_sets(calibration))
final_pool  <- pruned |> filter(keep) |> pull(item)

saveRDS(list(pruned = pruned, final_pool = final_pool),
        "cache/structure_irt.rds")

# Chapter 18: the hierarchical solution of the final pool and its
# bootstrap; the composites of its communities, bootstrapped at each wave
final_T0   <- items_at(df, "T0", final_pool)
assignment <- hier_ega(final_T0, hier_seeds[["T0"]]) |>
  hier_assignment() |>
  arrange(higher, lower, item)
boot_final <- boot_hier_ega(final_T0)
composites <- composite_items(assignment)

boot_wave <- \(wave) boot_ega(composite_scores(df, composites, wave))
composite_boot <- tibble(wave = names(hier_seeds)) |>
  mutate(boot        = map(wave, boot_wave),
         n           = map_int(boot, \(b) b$EGA$n),
         dimensions  = map_int(boot, \(b) b$EGA$n.dim),
         stability   = map(boot, item_stability),
         consistency = map(boot, structural_consistency),
         frequency   = map(boot, \(b) as_tibble(b$frequency))) |>
  select(-boot)

saveRDS(list(assignment     = assignment,
             final_items    = hier_item_stability(boot_final),
             final_lower    = structural_consistency(boot_final,
                                                     "lower_order"),
             final_higher   = structural_consistency(boot_final,
                                                     "higher_order"),
             composite_boot = composite_boot),
        "cache/structure_final.rds")




# Exploratory graph analysis (Chapters 16 and 18). The network of the items
# comes from the graphical lasso on pairwise correlations ("auto": Pearson
# for items with eleven answer categories); walktrap finds its communities,
# louvain the two levels of the hierarchical solution. Bootstraps draw 500
# samples from a normal distribution with the observed correlations, with
# seed 42; each hierarchical solution has a seed of its own per wave.
# Louvain draws random numbers (also when EGA checks a sample for a single
# dimension), which parallel workers do not seed: the bootstraps run in one
# process (ncores = 1), so that they repeat exactly.

# the label of an item's scale (needs `scales`, Chapter 2)
scale_label <- \(item) {
  scales$label[match(str_remove(item, "[0-9]+$"), scales$scale)]
}

# the answers of one wave to some items
items_at <- \(data, wave, items) {
  data |>
    filter(Occasion == wave) |>
    select(all_of(items))
}

# a bootstrap of the network and its communities
boot_ega <- \(items) {
  set.seed(42)
  bootEGA(items, iter = 500, type = "parametric", corr = "auto",
          model = "glasso", algorithm = "walktrap", na.data = "pairwise",
          seed = 42, ncores = 1, verbose = FALSE, plot.itemStability = FALSE)
}

# how often each item falls into its own community across the bootstrap
# samples; community = the community in the observed data
item_stability <- \(boot, level = NULL) {
  s <- itemStability(boot, IS.plot = FALSE)
  if (!is.null(level)) s <- s[[level]]
  stability <- s$item.stability$empirical.dimensions
  tibble(item      = names(stability),
         community = as.integer(s$membership$empirical[item]),
         stability = unname(stability))
}

# drop the items below the rule and bootstrap the rest again, until every
# item reaches the rule (at most 25 passes); returns each pass and the
# stability of the items that stay
converge_ega <- \(items, rule = .60, pass = 1) {
  stability <- item_stability(boot_ega(items))
  dropped   <- stability$item[stability$stability < rule]
  this_pass <- tibble(pass, items_in = ncol(items),
                      below = length(dropped),
                      min_stability  = min(stability$stability),
                      mean_stability = mean(stability$stability),
                      dropped = list(dropped))
  if (length(dropped) == 0 || pass == 25) {
    return(list(passes = this_pass, stability = stability))
  }
  rest <- converge_ega(select(items, -all_of(dropped)), rule, pass + 1)
  rest$passes <- bind_rows(this_pass, rest$passes)
  rest
}

# hierarchical EGA of one wave: communities of items (lower order) and
# communities of the community scores (higher order)
hier_seeds <- c(T0 = 123, T1 = 456, T2 = 789, T3 = 101112)

hier_ega <- \(items, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  hierEGA(items, scores = "network", loading.method = "revised",
          corr = "auto", na.data = "pairwise", model = "glasso",
          plot.EGA = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
}

hier_assignment <- \(hier) {
  hier$dim.variables |>
    as_tibble() |>
    transmute(item = items, lower = as.integer(lower),
              higher = as.integer(higher))
}

hier_size <- \(hier) {
  tibble(lower  = hier$lower_order$n.dim,
         higher = hier$higher_order$n.dim,
         TEFI   = hier$TEFI)
}

# the share of item pairs that two partitions treat alike (both together or
# both apart): 1 if the partitions are the same, whatever their numbers
pair_agreement <- \(a, b) {
  together_a <- outer(a, a, "==")
  together_b <- outer(b, b, "==")
  mean((together_a == together_b)[upper.tri(together_a)])
}

# a bootstrap of the hierarchical solution
boot_hier_ega <- \(items) {
  set.seed(42)
  bootEGA(items, iter = 500, type = "parametric", corr = "auto",
          model = "glasso", na.data = "pairwise", EGA.type = "hierEGA",
          scores = "network", loading.method = "revised", seed = 42,
          ncores = 1, verbose = FALSE, plot.itemStability = FALSE)
}

# item stability at both levels, in the order of the communities
hier_item_stability <- \(boot) {
  inner_join(item_stability(boot, "lower_order"),
             item_stability(boot, "higher_order"),
             by = "item", suffix = c("_lower", "_higher")) |>
    rename(lower = community_lower, higher = community_higher) |>
    arrange(higher, lower, desc(stability_lower))
}

# how often each community is found again with exactly the same items
structural_consistency <- \(boot, level = NULL) {
  s <- dimensionStability(boot, IS.plot = FALSE)
  if (!is.null(level)) s <- s[[level]]
  consistency <- s$dimension.stability$structural.consistency
  tibble(community   = as.integer(names(consistency)),
         consistency = unname(consistency))
}




# shares of the bootstrap samples as dots, one row per item or community,
# in panels; dashed: the criterion
plot_shares <- \(shares, criterion, x_label) {
  shares |>
    ggplot(aes(x = share, y = fct_rev(fct_inorder(label)))) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = criterion, colour = "grey60", linetype = 2) +
    geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", size = 2.2) +
    facet_grid(panel ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(x = x_label, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0))
}

Every wave enters with all its questionnaires, from 358 at T0 to 211 at T3; missing answers are handled pairwise.
Next → Step 2, the method and the criterion: How is the structure found, and how are two waves compared?


Step 2 · The method and the criterion each wave
How is the structure found, and how are two waves compared? hierEGA groups the items into communities (lower order), scores each person on each community from the network, and groups the community scores into factors (higher order); louvain finds both levels. Louvain visits the items in random order, so each wave gets a seed of its own. TEFI compares the solutions of the same items; lower is better. The numbers of the factors are arbitrary within each wave, so a later wave is compared with T0 by the Rand index: for every pair of items, are the two in the same factor or not, at T0 and at the later wave? The share of pairs on which the waves agree is 1 when the partition repeats exactly.
Next → Step 3, the estimation: How is it run?


Step 3 · The estimation each wave
How is it run? hierEGA once per wave, each wave with its seed:

wave_seeds <- c(T0 = 123, T1 = 456, T2 = 789, T3 = 101112)

hier <- map2(hier_answers, wave_seeds, \(answers, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  hierEGA(answers, scores = "network", loading.method = "revised",
          corr = "auto", na.data = "pairwise", model = "glasso",
          plot.EGA = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
})

The number of communities and factors at each wave, and the community and factor of every item:

hier_sizes <- hier |>
  map(\(h) tibble(lower  = h$lower_order$n.dim,
                  higher = h$higher_order$n.dim,
                  TEFI   = h$TEFI)) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "wave")

hier_by_wave <- hier |>
  map(\(h) h$dim.variables |>
        as_tibble() |>
        transmute(item = items, lower = as.integer(lower),
                  higher = as.integer(higher))) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "wave")

Next → Step 2, the method and the criterion: How robust is the T0 structure?


Step 2 · The method and the criterion January
How robust is the T0 structure? The bootstrap repeats hierEGA on 500 parametric samples, with seed 42. Besides the stability of every item at both levels, it reports each community’s and each factor’s structural consistency: the share of samples in which it reappears with exactly the same items. Values of .75 and above count as stable. The bootstrap compares each sample with its own hierEGA of the observed T0 answers. Louvain visits the items in random order, and this run has a seed of its own, so its communities can differ in detail from those of the T0 solution above.
Next → Step 3, the estimation: How does the script run it?

hier_higher <- structural_consistency(boot_hier, "higher_order")

title: 17. Redundancy and item response theory
text:
17.1 How each analysis is examined
Which models, and which rules? Each community of stable items from the bootstrap of the hierarchical solution (Chapter 16) gets a unidimensional graded response model (GRM; Samejima, 1969). For each item it estimates a discrimination a, how sharply the item’s answers change with the person’s standing on the community, and thresholds b, the standings at which a higher answer becomes more likely than a lower one. A GRM needs at least three items; items of smaller communities have no a. Unique variable analysis (UVA; Christensen et al., 2023) looks for redundancy in the network of all stable items: two items are redundant when their weighted topological overlap reaches .25, that is, when they are linked to the same other items with similar strength, so that one of them says nothing new.
What happens in each analysis? The same six steps, in the same order and in three parts: the analysis, its result, and what follows. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.

  end

The six steps in detail:
The analysis:

The starting point. Which items and which questionnaires enter: at T0 the questionnaires that answer every stable item, so that all models rest on the same persons; at the later waves the questionnaires of that wave that answer every stable item.
The rule. When an item leaves. An item with a discrimination below .50 at T0 goes. Of each redundant set, the item with the highest discrimination stays; ties go to the item with the higher bootstrap stability, then to the first in the alphabet. The models at the later waves apply no rule of their own: they show whether the verdict of T0 holds over the year.
The estimation. The models, written out: one GRM per community and wave, one UVA on all stable items.

The result:

The result. Discriminations and marginal reliabilities, thresholds, test information and trait scores, the redundant sets and the item each set keeps.
Where it strains. Estimates at the edge of what a model can identify, models that do not converge, and decisions that rest on a tie.

What follows:

What follows. Which items stay, and where they go next.

title: 17. Redundancy and item response theory
text:
17.2 Data and tools
Which data? The questionnaires of all four waves, and the communities and item stabilities from the bootstrap of Chapter 16:

ega         <- readRDS("cache/structure_ega.rds")    # Chapter 16
communities <- ega$hier_items |>
  select(item, community = lower, stability = stability_lower)

Which tools? The analysis of each step is written out below. The pipeline script runs the same two rules with the functions of R/structure_irt.R and stores the final pool that Chapter 18 reads; both are shown here, together with the wording of the items:

Pipeline scriptScript functionsItem wording



# Post hoc psychometrics: the bootstraps and the chain of item selections
# of Chapters 16 to 18. The T0 questionnaires calibrate every step; the
# composites are bootstrapped again at each wave.
# Run from swt-website/ after Chapter 2:  Rscript scripts/structure_pipeline.R

source("R/packages.R")
source("R/settings.R")
df <- readRDS("cache/df.rds")           # one row per questionnaire (Chapter 2)
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))
source("R/structure_pool.R")            # item pruning (Chapter 15)
source("R/structure_ega.R")             # network analyses (Chapter 16)
source("R/structure_irt.R")             # redundancy and IRT (Chapter 17)
source("R/structure_composites.R")      # composites (Chapter 18)

# Chapter 16: bootstrap until every item is stable, then bootstrap the
# hierarchical solution of the stable items. The items are ordered by
# community and stability; louvain and the bootstrap draws depend on the
# order of the items.
pool      <- structure_pool(df)
converged <- converge_ega(items_at(df, "T0", pool))
stable    <- converged$stability |>
  arrange(community, desc(stability)) |>
  pull(item)
boot_hier <- boot_hier_ega(items_at(df, "T0", stable))

saveRDS(list(pool        = pool,
             passes      = converged$passes,
             stability   = converged$stability,
             stable      = stable,
             hier_items  = hier_item_stability(boot_hier),
             hier_lower  = structural_consistency(boot_hier, "lower_order"),
             hier_higher = structural_consistency(boot_hier, "higher_order")),
        "cache/structure_ega.rds")

# Chapter 17: GRM per community and UVA on the persons who answered all
# stable items; the communities come from the bootstrap above
communities <- hier_item_stability(boot_hier) |>
  select(item, community = lower, stability = stability_lower)
calibration <- items_at(df, "T0", communities$item) |> drop_na()
pruned      <- community_discrimination(calibration, communities) |>
  prune_items(redundant_sets(calibration))
final_pool  <- pruned |> filter(keep) |> pull(item)

saveRDS(list(pruned = pruned, final_pool = final_pool),
        "cache/structure_irt.rds")

# Chapter 18: the hierarchical solution of the final pool and its
# bootstrap; the composites of its communities, bootstrapped at each wave
final_T0   <- items_at(df, "T0", final_pool)
assignment <- hier_ega(final_T0, hier_seeds[["T0"]]) |>
  hier_assignment() |>
  arrange(higher, lower, item)
boot_final <- boot_hier_ega(final_T0)
composites <- composite_items(assignment)

boot_wave <- \(wave) boot_ega(composite_scores(df, composites, wave))
composite_boot <- tibble(wave = names(hier_seeds)) |>
  mutate(boot        = map(wave, boot_wave),
         n           = map_int(boot, \(b) b$EGA$n),
         dimensions  = map_int(boot, \(b) b$EGA$n.dim),
         stability   = map(boot, item_stability),
         consistency = map(boot, structural_consistency),
         frequency   = map(boot, \(b) as_tibble(b$frequency))) |>
  select(-boot)

saveRDS(list(assignment     = assignment,
             final_items    = hier_item_stability(boot_final),
             final_lower    = structural_consistency(boot_final,
                                                     "lower_order"),
             final_higher   = structural_consistency(boot_final,
                                                     "higher_order"),
             composite_boot = composite_boot),
        "cache/structure_final.rds")




# Redundancy and item response theory (Chapters 17 and 18). A graded
# response model (GRM) per community gives each item its discrimination a;
# unique variable analysis (UVA) finds pairs of items so close in the
# network that one of them says nothing new.

# a unidimensional GRM on the persons who answered every item
grm_fit <- \(items) {
  mirt(drop_na(items), 1, itemtype = "graded", verbose = FALSE)
}

discrimination <- \(fit) {
  a <- coef(fit, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "a"]
  tibble(item = names(a), a = unname(a))
}

# the discrimination of every item, from one GRM per community; a GRM
# needs at least three items, so items of smaller communities get NA
community_discrimination <- \(items, communities) {
  grm <- communities |>
    filter(n() >= 3, .by = community) |>
    summarise(fit = list(grm_fit(items[item])), .by = community) |>
    mutate(reliability = map_dbl(fit, marginal_rxx),
           a           = map(fit, discrimination)) |>
    select(community, reliability, a) |>
    unnest(a)
  communities |>
    left_join(grm, by = c("community", "item"))
}

# sets of redundant items: a weighted topological overlap of .25 or more
redundant_sets <- \(items) {
  uva <- UVA(items, uva.method = "MBR", cut.off = .25, reduce = FALSE,
             verbose = FALSE)
  imap(uva$redundant, \(partners, item) sort(unique(c(item, partners))))
}

# from a redundant set keep the item with the highest discrimination, then
# the highest bootstrap stability, then the first in the alphabet
keep_one <- \(set, items) {
  items |>
    filter(item %in% set) |>
    arrange(desc(a), desc(stability), item) |>
    slice(1) |>
    pull(item)
}

# the items that stay: drop the poorly discriminating (a < .50) and all but
# one item of each redundant set; items has item, a and stability
prune_items <- \(items, sets) {
  redundant <- map(sets, \(set) setdiff(set, keep_one(set, items))) |>
    list_c()
  items |>
    mutate(poor = !is.na(a) & a < .50,
           redundant = item %in% redundant,
           keep = !poor & !redundant)
}

# the thresholds of each item of a GRM: b1, b2, ..., the trait levels at
# which an answer above a category becomes more likely than one at or below
thresholds <- \(fit) {
  coef(fit, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items |>
    as_tibble(rownames = "item") |>
    select(item, starts_with("b")) |>
    pivot_longer(-item, names_to = "threshold", values_to = "b",
                 values_drop_na = TRUE)
}

# the information of all items of a GRM together, over the trait levels
test_information <- \(fit, theta = seq(-4, 4, by = .1)) {
  tibble(theta = theta, information = testinfo(fit, matrix(theta)))
}




# The wording of every item (English version of the questionnaire), under
# the names of the analysis file (Chapter 2), and the reverse-keyed items

need <- \(numbers) paste0("needSatisfaction", numbers)
wording_names <- c(
  "Alienation1" = "NoAlienation1", "Alienation2" = "NoAlienation2",
  "Isolation1"  = "NoIsolation1",  "Isolation2"  = "NoIsolation2",
  set_names(paste0("AutonomySatisfaction",     1:4), need(c(1, 7, 13, 19))),
  set_names(paste0("AutonomyNonFrustrated",    1:4), need(c(2, 8, 14, 20))),

  set_names(paste0("CompetenceNonFrustrated",  1:4), need(c(6, 12, 18, 24)))
)

  transmute(item = coalesce(wording_names[column_name], column_name),
            text = str_squish(label_en))

         reliability = map_dbl(fit, marginal_rxx),

           coef(f, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items |>

Next → Step 2, the rule: When is an item redundant, and which item stays?


Step 2 · The rule January
When is an item redundant, and which item stays? Two items are redundant when their weighted topological overlap (wTO) in the network reaches .25; items linked in this way form a redundant set. Of each set, the item with the highest discrimination stays; ties go to the item with the higher bootstrap stability, then to the first in the alphabet.
Next → Step 3, the estimation: How is it run?


Step 3 · The estimation January
How is it run? UVA on the network of the complete T0 answers, with the cutoff of .25; each redundant set is an item with its partners:

uva <- UVA(calibration, uva.method = "MBR", cut.off = .25,
           reduce = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

red_sets <- uva$redundant |>
  imap(\(partners, item) sort(unique(c(item, partners))))

title: 13. Movers
text:
13.1 How each score is examined
What happens to each score? The two scales of Hypothesis 2 whose means barely moved (Chapter 9) go through the same seven steps, in the same order and in three parts: the score, the movers, and the verdict. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph SCORE["the score"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>the score"] --> S2["<b>Step 2</b><br>the bands"]
  end
  subgraph MOVERS["the movers: both groups"]
    direction LR
    S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>T0 to T1"] --> S4["<b>Step 4</b><br>from baseline"]
    S4 --> S5{{"<b>Step 5</b><br>each group in<br>its own window"}}
  end
  V["<b>Steps 6 and 7</b><br>the verdict, what follows"]
  SCORE --> MOVERS
  MOVERS --> V
  classDef both fill:#f0eaf8,stroke:#8e6bbf,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef all fill:#efeff2,stroke:#8a8a8a,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f
  class S1,S2 all
  class S3,S4,S5 both
  class V verdict
  style SCORE fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style MOVERS fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a






The seven steps in detail:
The score:

The score. Which items enter the score, and how reliable they are in January: Cronbach’s α of all T0 questionnaires. Tolerance Diversity enters with its 5 items, Women Attitude with all 9, including the two items at the ceiling that the score of Chapter 2 leaves out (womenAttitude_full, Chapter 2.3), so that a change on any item counts.
The bands. A person’s change is the score after minus the score before, for the persons who answered at both waves, here from T0 to T1. Three criteria draw the line between change and no change:

strict: any difference counts;
item step: more than one step on one item, 1/k of the scale for k items;
reliable change (Jacobson & Truax, 1991): more than 1.96 · SDbefore · √(2(1 − α)), with the standard deviation of the scores before, over the persons who answered at both waves, and α of step 1. A change beyond this band is unlikely (p < .05) to come from measurement error alone.

A figure shows the change of every person against the band of reliable change.

The movers:

Movers while the experimental group trains. The share of each group that increased, stayed the same or decreased from T0 to T1, under each of the three criteria.
Movers from baseline. The persons who answered at all four waves (S1, Chapter 3), from T0 to each later wave, under the strict criterion: do the two groups drift apart over the year?
Each group in its own training window. On the same persons, so that both windows rest on the same people: the share who improved (strict criterion) in each condition, from T0 to T1, while the experimental group trains, and from T2 to T3, while the control group trains. The two shares are compared by a two-proportion χ² test without continuity correction; a difference counts as significant at p < .05. The test needs an expected count of at least 5 in every cell (Cochran, 1954), checked for both windows. A figure shows both windows.

The verdict:

The verdict. Whether the group in training improves more often than the waiting group in both windows, as an effect of the training would predict, and whether either difference is significant.
What follows. How the result stands beside the Δd of Chapter 9 and, where Chapter 7 carries the scale on, the latent difference-in-differences of Chapter 11, and where it goes next.

title: 13. Movers
text:
13.2 Data and tools
Which data? The January questionnaires for the reliability (step 1), all questionnaires for the changes from T0 to T1 (steps 2 and 3), the questionnaires of the persons who answered at all four waves (steps 4 to 6), and the effects of the two scales in Chapters 9 and 11 for step 7:

t0       <- filter(df, Occasion == "T0")
complete <- filter(df, s1_complete)
means    <- readRDS("cache/means.rds")   # Δd (Chapter 9)
smm      <- readRDS("cache/smm.rds")     # latent DiD (Chapter 11)

127 persons answered at all four waves, once at each.
Which tools? The analysis of each step is written out for both scales. Only the two figures use small functions, defined once here; the wording of the items comes from the file that Chapter 6 shows:

ChangesRatesExpected countsItem wording



# the change of every person, one bar per step on one item and one panel
# per condition; shaded the band of reliable change
plot_changes <- \(changes, band, k) {
  changes |>
    ggplot(aes(change, fill = condition)) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -band, xmax = band, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
             fill = "grey85", alpha = .6) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 1 / k, center = 0) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linewidth = .3) +
    facet_wrap(~ condition, ncol = 1) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(Control = "#2a78d6",
                                 Experimental = "#eb6834"),
                      guide = "none") +
    labs(x = "change of the score, after minus before (scale 0 to 10)",
         y = "persons") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}




# the share of each group who improved, in the two training windows
plot_rates <- \(rates) {
  rates |>
    mutate(window = if_else(pre == "T0",
                            "T0 to T1\nthe experimental group trains",
                            "T2 to T3\nthe control group trains")) |>
    ggplot(aes(window, improved_percent, fill = condition)) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = .7), width = .6) +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f %%", improved_percent)),
              position = position_dodge(width = .7), vjust = -.4,
              size = 3.3) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(Control = "#2a78d6",
                                 Experimental = "#eb6834")) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 60), labels = \(x) str_c(x, " %")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "improved (strict criterion)", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}




# the counts a two-proportion test expects in its four cells (improved or
# not, by condition) if both groups improved equally often; the test needs
# at least 5 in every cell (Cochran, 1954)
expected_counts <- \(window) {
  observed <- cbind(improved = window$improved,
                    other    = window$persons - window$improved)
  outer(rowSums(observed), colSums(observed)) / sum(observed)
}

Next → Step 7, what follows: Where does the result go from here?


Step 7 · What follows
Where does the result go from here? Its rates enter the table at the end of this chapter (13.4), from which Chapter 20 counts the significant mover contrasts among the limits of the results. The means tell a similar story: on the score without the two items at the ceiling, the Δd of Chapter 9 is not significant while the experimental group trains (p = .094); while the control group trains it is (p = .022), but not after the correction for multiple testing (pBH = .096). A latent difference-in-differences does not exist for this scale: Women Attitude stops in Chapter 7, where no measurement model of the control group is possible. The mover analysis points the same way as the Δd, but adds no evidence of an effect of the training on Women Attitude.

title: 14. Robustness across sample sets
text:
14.1 How each effect is examined
What happens to each effect? The outcomes are the 23 scale scores and the three hypothesis composites (Chapter 2). Each goes through the same five steps, in the same order and in three parts: the effect in every set, the multilevel model, and the verdict. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph SETS["the effect in every set: both groups"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>Δd in every set"] --> S2["<b>Step 2</b><br>another standard<br>deviation"]
  end
  subgraph MLM["the multilevel model: the composites"]
    direction LR
    S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>the model of<br>Chapter 10 in every set"]
  end
  V{{"<b>Step 4</b><br>the verdict:<br>robust in all nine?"}} --> W["<b>Step 5</b><br>what follows"]
  SETS --> MLM
  MLM --> V
  classDef both fill:#f0eaf8,stroke:#8e6bbf,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f
  class S1,S2,S3 both
  class V,W verdict
  style SETS fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style MLM fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a






The five steps in detail:
The effect in every set:

Δd in every set. The Δd of Chapter 9 (Step 2): the change of the experimental group minus the change of the control group, each in standard deviations before the window, with its z-test; significant at p < .05. It is computed in each of the nine sample sets (14.2): for the scales in the two training windows, T0 to T1, while the experimental group trains (expected positive), and T2 to T3, while the control group trains (expected negative, as the freshly trained control group gains more); for the composites also from T0 to T2 and from T0 to T3, as in Chapter 9. Δd rests on the persons who answered at both waves of a window, so a set changes it only where it leaves out some of these pairs. A figure shows Δd with its interval in every set, the decision of Step 4 at a glance.
Another standard deviation. The same Δd with the standard deviation of all questionnaires of the group at the first wave of the window (Chapter 9, Step 3). This standard deviation changes with every set that leaves out questionnaires of that wave, even where the pairs stay the same; in S1, where every person answered at every wave, the two nearly coincide. The question is whether a verdict (p < .05) changes.

The multilevel model:

The multilevel model in every set. For the three composites, the preregistered outcomes: the model of Chapter 10, outcome ~ Occasion * condition + (1 | Municipality/id), refitted in each set, with its three interaction terms (the change from T0 to T1, T2 and T3, experimental minus control; expected positive at T1 and T2, and near zero at T3, after both groups have trained). The single scales are fitted once, on all questionnaires, in Chapter 10.

The verdict:

The verdict. In how many of the nine sets the effect is significantly positive and in how many significantly negative, in each window and under both standard deviations (for the composites also in the multilevel model). An effect counts as robust when it holds in the expected direction in all nine sets, under both standard deviations.
What follows. Where the result goes next, and what it amounts to.

The Δd of all outcomes in all sets is computed once, in 14.3; the scales follow by hypothesis block (14.4 to 14.6), then the composites (14.7), and 14.8 sets all effects side by side.

title: 14. Robustness across sample sets
text:
14.2 Data and tools
Which data? All questionnaires (df, Chapter 2) with the two flags of careless answering (Chapter 4), the three composites, their readable names, and the windows of Chapter 9:

df <- df |>
  left_join(select(careless, id, Occasion, s8_no_careless,
                   s9_no_careless_strict),
            by = c("id", "Occasion"))

composites <- c("H1_ListeningTogetherness", "H2_CognitiveComplexity",
                "H3_Wellbeing")

# readable names of the outcomes, the composites named by their hypothesis
outcome_labels <- c(set_names(scales$label, scales$scale),
                    H1_ListeningTogetherness = "Listening and Togetherness",
                    H2_CognitiveComplexity   = "Cognitive Complexity",
                    H3_Wellbeing             = "Well-being")

windows <- tribble(
  ~pre, ~post,
  "T0", "T1",
  "T0", "T2",
  "T0", "T3",
  "T2", "T3"
)

# the two training windows, in which the scales are compared
training_windows <- filter(windows, (pre == "T0" & post == "T1") |
                                    (pre == "T2" & post == "T3"))

Which questionnaires does each set keep? S0 to S6 come from the waves a person answered (Chapter 3), S8 and S9 from the screening for careless answering (Chapter 4). S7, the set without the paper forms entered twice, is the analysis file itself (Chapter 1):

sample_sets <- tribble(
  ~set, ~flag,                   ~definition,
  "S0", NA,                      "all questionnaires",
  "S1", "s1_complete",           "persons with all four waves",
  "S2", "s2_no_singletons",      "persons with at least two waves",
  "S3", "s3_has_T0",             "persons with a January questionnaire",
  "S4", "s4_T0_plus_post",       "January and a wave after the own training",
  "S5", "s5_group_baseline",     "both waves around the own training",
  "S6", "s6_no_T0_dropouts",     "not January only",
  "S8", "s8_no_careless",        "without careless answering (lenient flag)",
  "S9", "s9_no_careless_strict", "without careless answering (strict flag)"
)

# the questionnaires of a set (S0: all)
set_data <- \(flag) if (is.na(flag)) df else filter(df, .data[[flag]])

sample_sets <- sample_sets |>
  mutate(data           = map(flag, set_data),
         questionnaires = map_int(data, nrow),
         persons        = map_int(data, \(d) n_distinct(d$id)))

Which tools? The analysis of each step is written out for every outcome. Only the figure of Δd in every set and the path at the head of each outcome use small functions, defined once here:

SetsPath



# Δd with its 95 % interval in each set, one panel per window; filled
# points are significant (p < .05), open points are not
plot_sets <- \(effects) {
  effects |>
    mutate(set     = factor(set, levels = rev(sample_sets$set)),
           ci_low  = delta_d - qnorm(.975) * se,
           ci_high = delta_d + qnorm(.975) * se,
           test    = if_else(p < .05, "p < .05", "p ≥ .05")) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = delta_d, y = set, xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high,
               colour = test, fill = test)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = .3) +
    geom_linerange(linewidth = .5) +
    geom_point(shape = 21, size = 2.2, stroke = .6) +
    facet_wrap(~ window, nrow = 1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("p < .05" = "grey15",
                                   "p ≥ .05" = "grey55")) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("p < .05" = "grey15",
                                 "p ≥ .05" = "white")) +
    labs(x = "Δd, experimental minus control, with 95 % interval",
         y = NULL, colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}




# the path of an outcome through the five steps, from the tables of 14.3;
# for a composite, the model of Chapter 10 fitted once more in every set
effect_path <- \(name, next_text) {
  composite <- name %in% composites
  pairs  <- (if (composite) robust_delta_d else robust_scales) |>
    filter(outcome == name)
  all_sd <- (if (composite) robust_delta_d_all else robust_scales_all) |>
    filter(outcome == name)
  # the sets with a significant Δd in the expected direction
  holds <- \(effects, w, sign) {
    sum(effects$window == w & effects$p < .05 & sign * effects$delta_d > 0)
  }
  first  <- c(holds(pairs, "T0 to T1", 1), holds(all_sd, "T0 to T1", 1))
  second <- c(holds(pairs, "T2 to T3", -1), holds(all_sd, "T2 to T3", -1))
  changed <- sum((pairs$p < .05) != (all_sd$p < .05))
  multilevel <- if (composite) {
    t1 <- sample_sets$data |>
      map(\(d) lmer(as.formula(str_c(name, " ~ Occasion * condition + ",
                                      "(1 | Municipality/id)")),
                    data = d) |>
            tidy(effects = "fixed") |>
            filter(term == "OccasionT1:conditionExperimental")) |>
      list_rbind()
    str_c("T1: ", sum(t1$p.value < .05 & t1$estimate > 0),
          " of 9 sets significantly positive")
  } else "fitted once, on all questionnaires (Chapter 10)"
  tribble(
    ~Step, ~Question, ~Result, ~Next,
    "1", "In how many of the nine sets does Δd hold?",
    str_c("T0 to T1: ", first[1], " of 9 positive; T2 to T3: ", second[1],
          " of 9 negative"), "another SD",
    "2", "Same verdicts with the other standard deviation?",
    if (changed == 0) "yes, in every set and window" else {
      str_c("no: ", changed, " verdicts change")
    }, "multilevel model",
    "3", "The multilevel model in every set?", multilevel, "verdict",
    "4", "Robust: all nine sets, both standard deviations?",
    str_c("T0 to T1: ", if (all(first == 9)) "yes" else "no",
          "; T2 to T3: ", if (all(second == 9)) "yes" else "no"),
    "what follows",
    "5", "Where next?", next_text, "")
}

title: 14. Robustness across sample sets
text:
14.8 All effects at a glance
How robust is each effect? One row per outcome: the number of sets, out of nine, in which its Δd is significant in the expected direction, in the two training windows and under both standard deviations; the number in which it is significant against the training (standard deviation of the pairs, either window); and for the composites the sets with a significant T1 interaction in the multilevel model. The other tabs rank the scales, give the Δd and the interactions set by set, and compare the two standard deviations for the composites:

# the multilevel models of the three composites, set by set
robust_mlm <- bind_rows(h1_mlm, h2_mlm, h3_mlm) |>
  arrange(match(set, sample_sets$set))

# the Δd of all 26 outcomes in the two training windows, both SD
training_effects <- bind_rows(
  pairs = bind_rows(robust_scales, robust_delta_d),
  all   = bind_rows(robust_scales_all, robust_delta_d_all),
  .id = "SD") |>
  semi_join(training_windows, by = c("pre", "post")) |>
  mutate(expected = if_else(pre == "T0", delta_d > 0, delta_d < 0))

# per outcome, the sets with a significant effect as expected
set_counts <- training_effects |>
  mutate(column = if_else(SD == "pairs", window,
                          str_c(window, " (all SD)"))) |>
  summarise(sets = sum(p < .05 & expected), .by = c(outcome, column)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = column, values_from = sets)

# the sets with a significant effect against the training
against <- training_effects |>
  filter(SD == "pairs") |>
  summarise(against = sum(p < .05 & !expected), .by = outcome)

multilevel_T1 <- robust_mlm |>
  filter(wave == "T1") |>
  summarise(`multilevel T1` = sum(p < .05 & b > 0), .by = outcome)

glance <- set_counts |>
  left_join(against, by = "outcome") |>
  left_join(multilevel_T1, by = "outcome") |>
  mutate(block = coalesce(scales$block[match(outcome, scales$scale)],
                          "composite"),
         .before = 1)

The scales that hold in all nine sets stay the same with the standard deviation of all questionnaires. While the experimental group trains, the counts move by at most one set. No Alienation is the only outcome with an effect against the training, in eight sets while the experimental group trains.
Where an effect while the experimental group trains holds in eight of the nine sets, the set it misses is always S1, the smallest: so for seven outcomes, Cognitive Complexity among them. Of the composites, Cognitive Complexity holds in eight sets while the experimental group trains, as Δd and in the multilevel model; Listening and Togetherness and Well-being hold in three as Δd. title: 3. Sample
section: 3.1 How each part of the sample is examined
text:
3.1 How each part of the sample is examined
What happens to each part of the sample? The same six steps in three parts, always in the same order: the problem, the rule and the result. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph PROBLEM["the problem"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>what the data look like"] --> S2{{"<b>Step 2</b><br>the problem:<br>what could<br>mislead?"}}
  end
  subgraph RULE["the rule"]
    direction LR
    S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>the rule:<br>counted, tested<br>or defined"] --> S4["<b>Step 4</b><br>the evidence<br>per case"]
  end
  subgraph RESULT["the result"]
    direction LR
    S5["<b>Step 5</b><br>before and after"] --> S6["<b>Step 6</b><br>what follows"]
  end
  PROBLEM --> RULE
  RULE --> RESULT
  classDef all fill:#efeff2,stroke:#8a8a8a,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f
  class S1,S2,S3,S4,S5 all
  class S6 verdict
  style PROBLEM fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style RULE fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style RESULT fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a






The six steps in detail:
The problem:

What the data look like. The rows the part starts from: one row per questionnaire (df) or one row per person (df_wide), as Chapter 2 saved them.
The problem. What the rows do not tell directly, or could mislead about: persons who answered at different waves, waves that never arrived, missing answers on age or sex, groups that differ by chance.

The rule:

The rule. How the part is counted, tested or defined. A person counts once. The two conditions are compared with a Mann-Whitney U test for age, a χ² test with continuity correction for sex, and a χ² test for the waves attended, which is descriptive, because a person contributes up to four questionnaires; p < .05 counts as a difference. Each sample set is defined by the waves its persons attended.
The evidence per case. The counts behind the result: per municipality, per pattern of attendance, per person.

The result:

Before and after. What the rule changes: from questionnaires to persons, from January to December, from all questionnaires to a sample set.
What follows. Where the part goes next: the description of the participants in the Method section, the models of the later chapters, and the re-estimation of the training effects in Chapter 14.

title: 3. Sample
text:
3.2 Data and tools
Which data? One row per questionnaire (df) for everything counted per wave, one row per person (df_wide) for everything counted per person, and, for the patterns of attendance and the sample sets, the waves each person answered:

# the waves each person answered, as a pattern such as T0-T1-T3
person_patterns <- df |>
  arrange(id, Occasion) |>
  summarise(pattern = str_c(Occasion, collapse = "-"),
            .by = c(id, condition, Municipality))

Which tools? Every count and test is written out where it is used. Only the two figures use small functions, defined once here:

Persons per waveAge



# the persons answering at each wave, by condition
condition_colours <- c(Control = "#2a78d6", Experimental = "#eb6834")
plot_by_wave <- \(counts) {
  counts |>
    ggplot(aes(Occasion, persons, colour = condition, group = condition)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
    geom_point(size = 2.6) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = condition_colours) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "persons", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
}




# the age of the persons, one panel per condition
plot_age <- \(persons) {
  persons |>
    filter(!is.na(age)) |>
    ggplot(aes(age, fill = condition)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 2.5, boundary = 20, colour = "white") +
    facet_wrap(~ condition, ncol = 1) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = condition_colours, guide = "none") +
    labs(x = "age (mean of the ages given)", y = "persons") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

title: 4. Data quality
section: 4.1 How each screening step is examined
text:
4.1 How each screening step is examined
What happens in each step of the screening? The same six steps in three parts, always in the same order: the problem, the rule and the result. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph PROBLEM["the problem"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>what the data look like"] --> S2{{"<b>Step 2</b><br>the problem:<br>what does careless<br>answering leave?"}}
  end
  subgraph RULE["the rule"]
    direction LR
    S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>the rule:<br>index and cutoff"] --> S4["<b>Step 4</b><br>the evidence<br>per case"]
  end
  subgraph RESULT["the result"]
    direction LR
    S5["<b>Step 5</b><br>before and after:<br>how the count moves"] --> S6["<b>Step 6</b><br>what follows"]
  end
  PROBLEM --> RULE
  RULE --> RESULT
  classDef all fill:#efeff2,stroke:#8a8a8a,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f
  class S1,S2,S3,S4,S5 all
  class S6 verdict
  style PROBLEM fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style RULE fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style RESULT fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a






The six steps in detail:
The problem:

What the data look like. The answers the step looks at: the answers as they were ticked, in the order of the questionnaire, or the items as analysed, after Chapter 2 turned the reverse-keyed items around.
The problem. What careless answering leaves in these answers, and why attentive answering can look much the same.

The rule:

The rule. The index, written out, and the cutoff that marks a questionnaire: a run of 20 or more identical answers that passes a reverse-keyed item (long string); a distance of at least 2.5 SD above the block mean in two or more of six blocks (agreeing with opposites); an even-odd consistency below .30; a psychometric-synonyms correlation below .22. Three supplementary indicators (Mahalanobis p < .001, variability below the 2.5th percentile, more than 25 missing items) are reported but mark nothing. Two questionnaires count as entered twice when they agree on at least 95 % of at least 80 items answered in both and their answers vary.
The evidence per case. The questionnaires the rule marks, by pseudonym and wave, with the values that put them there.

The result:

Before and after. How many questionnaires the rule marks, and how that number moves with the cutoff, with the rule, or across the conditions and waves.
What follows. Where the result goes: into the two flags, the sample sets S8 and S9, and Chapter 14.

title: 4. Data quality
text:
4.2 Data and tools
Which data? One row per questionnaire. Most indicators of careless answering look at the answers as they were ticked, in the order of the questionnaire. Chapter 2 turned the 22 reverse-keyed items around; for the screening they are turned back. keyed holds the items as analysed, answers the answers as given. The columns of the data follow the order of the printed Serbian questionnaire.

# the 22 reverse-keyed items, under their names from Chapter 2
reversed_items <- c("NoAlienation1", "NoAlienation2",
                    "NoIsolation1", "NoIsolation2",
                    "Flourishing5", "Flourishing6", paste0("Rogerian", 7:9),
                    "ToleranceDiversity1",
                    str_subset(item_names, "NonFrustrated"))

# one row per questionnaire, the 102 items in the order of the questionnaire
keyed   <- df |> select(all_of(item_names))
answers <- keyed |> mutate(across(all_of(reversed_items), \(x) 10 - x))

Which tools? Every index is written out for its indicator. Only the figures use small functions, defined once here:

Answer sequenceOppositesWithin a questionnaireDistribution of an index



# the answers of some questionnaires as given, in the order of the
# questionnaire, one panel each in the order given; grey lines mark the
# reverse-keyed items
plot_sequence <- \(sequences) {
  sequences |>
    mutate(questionnaire = fct_inorder(questionnaire)) |>
    pivot_longer(-questionnaire, names_to = "item", values_to = "answer") |>
    mutate(position = match(item, item_names)) |>
    ggplot(aes(position, answer)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = which(item_names %in% reversed_items),
               colour = "grey85") +
    geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = .5) +
    geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", size = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
    facet_wrap(~ questionnaire, ncol = 1) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 5, 10)) +
    labs(x = "position in the questionnaire", y = "answer as given") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}




# the mean of the positive against the mean of the negative answers of each
# block, one point per questionnaire; on the grey line they add up to 10
plot_opposites <- \(means) {
  means |>
    filter(!is.na(positive), !is.na(negative)) |>
    ggplot(aes(positive, negative)) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 10, slope = -1, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", alpha = .3, size = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~ block, ncol = 3) +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 5, 10)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 5, 10)) +
    labs(x = "mean of the positive items (as given)",
         y = "mean of the negative items (as given)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}




# within single questionnaires: each value against its counterpart (the two
# halves of a scale, the two items of a pair), one panel per questionnaire
# in the order given; points on the grey line agree
plot_within <- \(points, x_label, y_label) {
  points |>
    filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
    mutate(questionnaire = fct_inorder(questionnaire)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
    geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
    geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", alpha = .6, size = 1.8,
               position = position_jitter(width = .1, height = .1,
                                          seed = 1)) +
    facet_wrap(~ questionnaire) +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 5, 10)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 5, 10)) +
    labs(x = x_label, y = y_label) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}




# an index over all questionnaires; red the questionnaires below the
# cutoff (dashed line)
plot_index <- \(index, cutoff, label) {
  tibble(index) |>
    filter(!is.na(index)) |>
    ggplot(aes(index, fill = index < cutoff)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = .05, boundary = cutoff) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = cutoff, linetype = "dashed") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#2a78d6", `TRUE` = "#e34948"),
                      guide = "none") +
    labs(x = label, y = "questionnaires") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

4.3 Indicators of careless answering
Which indicators? The four preregistered indicators, each looking for one trace of careless answering: long strings of the same answer, agreeing with an item and with its opposite, and two kinds of inconsistent profile (even-odd consistency and psychometric synonyms). Three supplementary indicators follow; they are reported but mark nothing.

Long strings

The problem · Steps 1 and 2

Step 1 · What the data look like all questionnaires
In which order were the items answered? The 102 items stand in the order of the printed questionnaire. Between the reverse-keyed items lie stretches of items that are all worded the same way:

# the position of every item in the questionnaire
item_order <- tibble(position = seq_along(item_names), item = item_names,
                     reversed = item %in% reversed_items)

# stretches of items without a reverse-keyed item, from two items on
item_order |>
  mutate(stretch = consecutive_id(reversed)) |>
  filter(!reversed) |>
  summarise(from = first(item), to = last(item), items = n(),
            .by = stretch) |>

The widest stretch runs over 27 items, from Paradox Mindset 1 to Flourishing 4. In the 24 need-satisfaction items at the end, a positively worded and a reverse-keyed item alternate.
Next → Step 2, the problem: How long are the runs, wherever they fall?


Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
How long are the runs, wherever they fall? A run is a series of identical answers in the order of the questionnaire; a missing answer ends a run. Every run of every questionnaire, and the longest run of each:

# every run of identical answers, one row per run; a missing answer (set to
# -1 here) ends a run and is no run itself
ls_runs <- as.matrix(answers) |>
  asplit(1) |>
  map(\(answer) rle(replace_na(as.vector(answer), -1))) |>
  map(\(r) tibble(length = r$lengths, value = r$values,
                  end = cumsum(r$lengths))) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "row") |>
  mutate(start = end - length + 1) |>
  filter(value != -1)

# the longest run of each questionnaire (NA for one without any answer)
ls_any <- tibble(row = seq_len(nrow(answers))) |>
  left_join(summarise(ls_runs, longest = max(length), .by = row),
            by = "row") |>
  pull(longest)

tibble(ls_any) |>
  describe(ls_any)


Descriptive Statistics
----------------------

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Variable    Mean  Median     SD   Range    IQR  Skewness     N  Missing
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  ls_any    10.418   9.000  4.898  47.000  3.000     2.630  1140        0
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------


Long runs are common: 515 questionnaires have a run of ten or more identical answers somewhere, 35 one of 20 or more. Within a stretch of items worded the same way, such a run is what an attentive person who agrees with all of them gives as well. Careless answering shows where a run goes on across a reverse-keyed item, where an attentive person would switch sides.
Next → Step 3, the rule: Which runs count?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
Which runs count? Only runs that pass a reverse-keyed item. The index is the longest such run; a run of 20 or more marks a long string:

# the positions of the 22 reverse-keyed items in the questionnaire
reversed_at <- which(item_names %in% reversed_items)

# does a run pass one of them?
ls_runs <- ls_runs |>
  mutate(through_reversed = map2_lgl(start, end, \(s, e)

Next → Step 2, the problem: Why does agreeing with both sides point to careless answering?


Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
Why does agreeing with both sides point to careless answering? An attentive person who agrees with the positive items of a block, ticking 9, say, disagrees with the negative ones and ticks about 1: the two means add up to about 10. Someone who agrees with both sides, or disagrees with both, ends far from 10. But the blocks are short (1 to 6 items per side) and differ in how far attentive answers usually stray from 10, so a distance says little by itself; it has to be large for its block.
Next → Step 3, the rule: How far from 10, and in how many blocks?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
How far from 10, and in how many blocks? The inconsistency of a block is the distance of the sum of the two means from 10. A block counts as inconsistent when it lies 2.5 SD above its own mean:

# per block: the distance of (mean of the positive + mean of the negative
# answers) from 10
inconsistency <- mixed_blocks |>
  map(\(b) abs(rowMeans(answers[b$positive], na.rm = TRUE) +
                 rowMeans(answers[b$negative], na.rm = TRUE) - 10)) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) if_else(is.finite(x), x, NA)))

# distance from the block's own mean, in SD of the block
inconsistency_z <- inconsistency |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) as.vector(scale(x))))

How inconsistent is a block usually?

tibble(block  = names(mixed_blocks),
       M      = map_dbl(inconsistency, \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
       SD     = map_dbl(inconsistency, \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
       cutoff = M + 2.5 * SD,
       above  = map_int(inconsistency_z, \(z) sum(z >= 2.5, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

Next → Step 2, the problem: Do the two halves of each scale tell the same story?


Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
Do the two halves of each scale tell the same story? An attentive person who rates high on a scale does so in both of its halves, and low in both where they rate low. Across the scales, their odd-half means follow their even-half means. Careless answers break that link: the halves of one scale no longer agree, and the profile of one half says little about the other.
Next → Step 3, the rule: How is the agreement of the halves measured?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
How is the agreement of the halves measured? The index is the correlation of the odd-half and the even-half means across the scales, within one questionnaire, stepped up to full length with the Spearman-Brown formula. It needs at least ten scales with both halves, and halves that vary; below .30 marks a questionnaire:

# the mean of the odd and of the even items of each scale, per questionnaire
odd <- items_by_scale |>
  map(\(items) rowMeans(keyed[items[seq_along(items) %% 2 == 1]],
                        na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  as_tibble()
even <- items_by_scale |>
  map(\(items) rowMeans(keyed[items[seq_along(items) %% 2 == 0]],
                        na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  as_tibble()

# within each questionnaire, the correlation of the two halves across the
# scales answered in both
r_halves <- map_dbl(seq_len(nrow(keyed)), \(i) {
  a  <- unlist(odd[i, ])
  b  <- unlist(even[i, ])
  ok <- is.finite(a) & is.finite(b)
  if (sum(ok) < 10 || sd(a[ok]) == 0 || sd(b[ok]) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  cor(a[ok], b[ok])
})

# stepped up to the full length (Spearman-Brown)
even_odd <- if_else(r_halves <= -1, -1, 2 * r_halves / (1 + r_halves))

What else could point to careless answering? Three further signs, each of which has an innocent reading as well. Next → Step 3, the rule: How are they computed?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
How are they computed? The Mahalanobis distance needs complete answers: missing answers are replaced by the item median, for questionnaires with at most ten missing items. The IRV is the standard deviation of a questionnaire’s answers as given:

# Mahalanobis distance: missing answers replaced by the item median, for
# questionnaires with at most ten missing items
imputed   <- keyed |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) replace_na(x, median(x, na.rm = TRUE))))
mahad_p   <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(keyed))
mahad_p[n_missing <= 10] <- imputed[n_missing <= 10, ] |>
  mahad(plot = FALSE) |>
  pchisq(df = ncol(keyed), lower.tail = FALSE)

title: 7. Measurement invariance over time and groups
text:
7.1 How each construct is examined
Why each group on its own? The experimental group was trained between January and March, the control group between September and December. If the training changes how people read an item, it does so at different waves in the two groups. A model of all persons together has one latent mean per wave and averages the two groups; it would blur such a change and push what it cannot describe into the residuals. So the question whether the measurement stays the same over time is asked in each group, and only then are the groups compared. Before the training both groups answer alike (Chapter 6, Step 7), which is why Chapter 6 settles the measurement models on the January questionnaires of both groups together.
What happens to each construct? Twelve steps in four parts, always in the same order: the model in all persons, each group on its own over the four waves, both groups together, and the verdict. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph ALL["all persons"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>the model"] --> S2{{"<b>Step 2</b><br>possible? does it fit?"}}
  end
  subgraph CON["control group"]
    direction TB
    C3{{"<b>Step 3</b><br>possible?"}} --> C4["<b>Step 4</b><br>loadings over time"]
    C4 --> C5["<b>Step 5</b><br>intercepts over time"]
  end
  subgraph EXP["experimental group"]
    direction TB
    E3{{"<b>Step 3</b><br>possible?"}} --> E4["<b>Step 4</b><br>loadings over time"]
    E4 --> E5["<b>Step 5</b><br>intercepts over time"]
  end
  subgraph BOTH["both groups"]
    direction LR
    B6{{"<b>Step 6</b><br>possible? misfit<br>from the groups?"}} --> B7["<b>Step 7</b><br>loadings across<br>the groups"]
    B7 --> B8["<b>Step 8</b><br>intercepts across<br>the groups"]
  end
  V["<b>Steps 9 to 12</b><br>verdict, partial invariance, alignment, what follows"]
  ALL --> CON
  ALL --> EXP
  CON --> BOTH
  EXP --> BOTH
  BOTH --> V
  classDef all fill:#efeff2,stroke:#8a8a8a,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef con fill:#e6f0fb,stroke:#2a78d6,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef exp fill:#fdece3,stroke:#eb6834,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef both fill:#f0eaf8,stroke:#8e6bbf,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f
  class S1,S2 all
  class C3,C4,C5 con
  class E3,E4,E5 exp
  class B6,B7,B8 both
  class V verdict
  style ALL fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style CON fill:#f7fafe,stroke:#2a78d6
  style EXP fill:#fff9f6,stroke:#eb6834
  style BOTH fill:#faf8fd,stroke:#8e6bbf






Two rules hold along the way. At each check (the hexagons), a model that is not possible stops, and the stop rule of Step 3 looks for the mildest change that makes it possible; if none does, the construct stops. At each test of equal loadings or intercepts (the boxes), a step that fails frees the item the score test names (Step 10); with two items that is not possible, and the construct stops.
How to read a construct below? It opens with its path through these steps, one row per step, and then takes them in the same four parts, each under its own heading (also in the table of contents on the left). The label beside each step names its data: all persons, control, experimental or both groups. Every step ends with what comes next.
The twelve steps in detail:
All persons:

The model. The items of Chapter 6 load on one factor per wave; the four factors are correlated, the residual covariances of Chapter 6 recur at every wave, and each item’s residual is correlated with itself across the waves (autocorrelated residuals; Little, 2013). Persons who missed a wave keep their other answers (full-information maximum likelihood, robust standard errors).

The scale of the factors. Each factor takes its scale from all of its items (effects coding; Little, Slegers & Card, 2006): the loadings average 1, and once the intercepts are held equal, they sum to 0. A latent mean then lies on the 0 to 10 scale of the answers, no single item serves as the reference, and the loading and the intercept of every item can be tested.
Two items. Both load 1 at every wave. The data leave no other choice: the autocorrelations of both items take up exactly the covariances that could tell the two loadings apart, so any ratio of the loadings fits equally well (Step 1 of Others Listen to Me shows it). For the same reason equal loadings cannot be tested: “the items load more strongly at T2” and “the factor varies more at T2” are the same model. With two items, the steps on the loadings are empty.

The configural model in all persons. Loadings and intercepts free at every wave, in all persons together. It goes through the eleven checks of Step 3. Whether one factor per wave describes the items is judged here, once, by a CFI of at least .90 in all persons: the groups hold half the persons each, and with up to 32 answers that alone lowers their fit (Moshagen, 2012; Step 6 shows it). Loadings and intercepts are not held equal here: whether they stay the same over time is asked in each group, since the groups were trained at different times.
In each group, the control group and then the experimental group:
The checks. Every configural model, in all persons, in each group and in both groups, goes through the same eleven checks, in the order of the textbooks (Brown, 2015, ch. 4; Kline, 2016, ch. 9):

Did the estimation work? (1) It converged.
Is the solution proper? (2) No residual variance is negative, (3) no correlation lies beyond ±1, (4) the residual and (5) the factor covariances are positive definite, and (6) every free parameter has a standard error. A model that fails one of these estimates something impossible and tests nothing.
How well does it fit overall? (7) The CFI, (8) the RMSEA with its 90 % interval, (9) the SRMR. The CFI decides once, in all persons (Step 2); in the groups it is reported.
Where does it strain? (10) The largest modification index.
Are the estimates sensible? (11) The smallest standardized loading, and in all persons the loadings of every item at every wave.

The models with equal loadings or intercepts (Steps 4, 5, 7 and 8) go through checks 1 to 6 as well; whether they fit is the question of the step itself.
When a model fails, it stops. First, the estimate at fault is examined, in the figure of the model and with its interval: does its interval reach into the possible range, and on how many persons does it rest (Kolenikov & Bollen, 2012)? Then the mildest change that makes all models possible is chosen, in this order, so that every step compares like with like:

A. The estimate at fault, and only there: a residual correlation beyond ±1 is set to 0, and a negative residual variance within sampling error is set to 0 together with the links of that residual to the other waves.
B. One autocorrelation per item, the same for every pair of waves: each item keeps its link over time, but only one.
C. For the comparison of the groups: each item’s residual variance the same in both groups.
D. No autocorrelations at all.
E. The items as ordinal, in three categories (up to 8, 9, 10), estimated by WLSMV with the identification of Wu and Estabrook (2016): for answers that pile up at the top of the scale.

If no change makes the models possible, the construct stops: it is not tested further, and its latent means are not compared in Chapter 11.
Loadings over time. Each loading keeps one value over the four waves.
Intercepts over time. Each intercept keeps one value over the four waves as well; the latent means are now free.
Both groups:
Do the groups add misfit? The configural models of both groups, fitted together, against the same model with the persons split at random three times. If the real groups fit as the random halves do, the groups add no misfit of their own.
Loadings across the groups. Each loading has the same value in both groups as well.
Intercepts across the groups. Each intercept has the same value in both groups as well. Only now are the latent means of all eight cells on one scale, which is what Chapter 11 compares.
Steps 4, 5, 7 and 8 each compare a model with the one before. A step holds when the CFI drops by no more than .010 and the RMSEA rises by no more than .015, the cutoffs Chen (2007) recommends for samples of more than 300. In models of a few hundred persons with missing waves the robust CFI is unstable, so these steps use the ML indices, and each also shows the scaled χ² difference test (Satorra & Bentler, 2001).
The verdict:
The verdict under both sets of cutoffs. The units of these models are the persons, but each group holds about 200 to 250, and each cell only those who answered at that wave, some fewer than 100. For samples of 300 or fewer, Chen (2007) reads a drop in CFI of at least .005, supplemented by a rise in RMSEA of at least .010 or in SRMR of at least .025 (loadings) or .005 (intercepts), as noninvariance. Here the CFI is the main criterion (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016): a step holds when the CFI drops by less than .005 and, in addition, the RMSEA or the SRMR stays within its limit. Chen’s cutoffs for more than 300 decide; the small-sample reading shows how firm the verdict is.
Partial invariance. Where a step fails, the score test shows whose equality costs most: the loadings or intercepts of that item, in that group, are freed, and the step is tested again, until it holds (Byrne et al., 1989). The search stops before fewer than two items would keep equal parameters. A freed item leaves the sum that scales the factor, and the partial model that holds is the model that goes on.
Alignment. Besides the tests, the preregistration names approximate invariance by alignment (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2014), as implemented in the package sirt. Alignment starts from the configural model, with the factor standardised in each of the eight cells, and searches the latent means and standard deviations under which the loadings and intercepts of the cells are as alike as possible, without forcing them to be equal. Two results: the share of loadings and intercepts more than .10 item standard deviations from their common aligned value (noninvariant), and how far the aligned means lie from those of the final model. Asparouhov and Muthén (2014) trust aligned means when no more than 25 % of the parameters are noninvariant.
What follows. The status of the construct (as specified, adjusted, partial, or stopped) and the model that goes on to Chapter 11.

The models of the steps. Within each group (Steps 3 to 5), and for both groups together (Steps 6 to 8), what each holds equal:

time_steps <- tribble(
  ~level,                 ~loadings, ~intercepts,
  "configural",           "free",    "free",
  "loadings over time",   "time",    "free",
  "intercepts over time", "time",    "time"
)

group_steps <- tribble(
  ~level,                     ~loadings, ~intercepts,
  "configural",               "free",    "free",
  "over time",                "time",    "time",
  "loadings across groups",   "groups",  "time",
  "intercepts across groups", "groups",  "groups"
)

How are the checks and the cutoffs computed?

# the two checks of every model; lavaan's own check of the solution looks
# for negative variances and for covariances that are not positive definite.
# A model that cannot be estimated at all (NULL) or does not converge is not
# possible
gates <- \(fit) {
  converged <- !is.null(fit) && lavInspect(fit, "converged")
  tibble(converged,
         admissible = converged &&
           isTRUE(suppressWarnings(lavInspect(fit, "post.check"))))
}

# the configural model fits with a CFI of at least .90, in all persons
fits_configural <- \(CFI) CFI >= .90

# Chen's (2007) cutoffs for more than 300 persons
holds_chen <- \(delta_CFI, delta_RMSEA) {
  delta_CFI >= -.010 & delta_RMSEA <= .015
}

# Chen's (2007) cutoffs for 300 or fewer, the CFI first; the SRMR limit is
# .025 for loadings and .005 for intercepts
holds_small <- \(level, delta_CFI, delta_RMSEA, delta_SRMR) {
  srmr_limit <- if_else(str_starts(level, "loadings"), .025, .005)
  delta_CFI >= -.005 & (delta_RMSEA <= .010 | delta_SRMR <= srmr_limit)
}
