title: 5. Reliability and baseline correlations
text:
5.1 How each scale is examined
What happens to each scale? The same four steps, in the same order, for each of the 23 scales (Chapter 2). Nothing in this chapter changes a scale: each keeps the items of its score, with the reverse-keyed items turned and Women Attitude without its two items at the ceiling. The four steps fall into three parts: the reliability at each wave, the correlations in January, and what follows. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph REL["reliability: all questionnaires of each wave"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>the items"] --> S2{{"<b>Step 2</b><br>α and ω per wave,<br>item checks"}}
  end
  subgraph COR["correlations: January"]
    direction LR
    S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>correlations with<br>the other scales"]
  end
  V["<b>Step 4</b><br>what follows"]
  REL --> COR
  COR --> V
  classDef all fill:#efeff2,stroke:#8a8a8a,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f
  class S1,S2,S3 all
  class V verdict
  style REL fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style COR fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a






The four steps in detail:
Reliability, at each wave:

The items. Which questions make up the scale, in their wording, and which of them were asked the other way round (reverse-keyed) and turned for the analysis.
α and ω per wave. How consistently the items measure, at each of the four waves, over all questionnaires of that wave. Cronbach’s α (psych::alpha(), its raw α) needs at least two items; it rests on the covariances of the answers as given, each pair of items on the questionnaires that answer both, as in Table 1. McDonald’s ω (psych::omega() with one factor, its total ω) needs at least three items; it lets the items measure the scale to different degrees and rests on their correlations, where every item counts the same. Values of .70 and more count as acceptable, values below .60 as poor. Where ω lies more than .05 above α, the step also shows how widely each item spreads: an item that spreads far more widely than the others weighs more in α, but not in ω. Then the item analysis of the textbooks (Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994; Clark & Watson, 1995): the average correlation between the items, which Clark and Watson put between .15 and .50 for a scale that is neither too broad nor redundant; each item’s correlation with the sum of the other items (the corrected item-total correlation), which should reach .30; and α without each item, which rises by more than .01 only for an item that goes less with the scale than the others. The checks are reported; none of them changes a scale here.

Correlations, in January:

Correlations with the other scales. How the score of the scale goes with the scores of the other 22 scales in January (T0), each pair on the questionnaires that answer both. A correlation is significant (p < .05, two-sided) from the critical |r| for the number of January questionnaires (5.2) on; it counts as moderate from .30, as strong from .50, and as small if it is significant but below .30. The sizes are judged on the unrounded r.

What follows:

What follows. Where the scale goes in the later chapters: its α into Table 1, its score into the analyses of the training effects, and its items into the latent factors of Chapter 6.

And the composites? The three hypothesis composites (5.6) go through the same four steps. Their second step asks in addition whether every item goes with the pool, and what α becomes on the questionnaires that answer every item; their third asks how closely the scales of the block hang together, and how the composite goes with the other two. Five further composites that cut across the blocks (5.7) have no score: they go through the first two steps and what follows. The chapter closes with all correlations side by side (5.8) and a table across all scales and composites (5.9).

title: 1. From Questionnaires to the Analysis File
section: 1.1 How each processing step is examined
text:
1.1 How each processing step is examined
What happens at each processing step? The same six steps in three parts, always in the same order: the problem, the rule and the result. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph PROBLEM["the problem"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>what the data look like"] --> S2{{"<b>Step 2</b><br>the problem:<br>what would distort<br>the analysis?"}}
  end
  subgraph RULE["the rule"]
    direction LR
    S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>the rule,<br>one code file"] --> S4["<b>Step 4</b><br>the evidence<br>per case"]
  end
  subgraph RESULT["the result"]
    direction LR
    S5["<b>Step 5</b><br>before and after"] --> S6["<b>Step 6</b><br>what follows"]
  end
  PROBLEM --> RULE
  RULE --> RESULT
  classDef all fill:#efeff2,stroke:#8a8a8a,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f
  class S1,S2,S3,S4,S5 all
  class S6 verdict
  style PROBLEM fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style RULE fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style RESULT fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a






The six steps in detail:
The problem:

What the data look like. The questionnaires as the processing step finds them: what the files, codes or answers hold, counted before anything changes. The step keeps a copy of this file (…_before) for the comparison in Step 5.
The problem. What would distort the analysis if the data stayed as they are: one person counted as two, two people counted as one, one paper form counted twice, or an answer that cannot be.

The rule:

The rule. The change, written once in a code file of its own (R/ch01_….R) and applied to every questionnaire alike. Where a rule rests on a list of cases, the file stops with the pseudonym of any listed case that is not found exactly as listed.
The evidence per case. Every case the rule touches, one line each, with the data it rests on; the paper forms were not available. Two codes count as one person if they lie in one municipality, differ in one part of the code (the letter, the month or the day) and give the same sex and an age within a year (a birthday may fall between two waves), or if the code written a second time, at the end of the questionnaire, names the other. Two questionnaires count as copies of one paper form if they agree in at least 95 % of the answers both give, with answers that vary over the scale.

The result:

Before and after. The questionnaires, persons and columns of the file before and after the processing step, and what changed for the cases of Step 4.
What follows. Where the result goes next: the next processing step, the sample of Chapter 3, the screening of Chapter 4, or the case log of the finished file.

title: 1. From Questionnaires to the Analysis File
text:
1.2 Data and tools
Which data? The 79 Excel files of the municipalities, one per municipality and wave, in the folder data/raw, and the private file that gives every participant code its pseudonym, data/pseudonyms.csv (both named in the settings above). Neither is published, as both hold the codes.

# the Excel files, without the lock files of open workbooks
questionnaire_files <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.xlsx$") |>
  str_subset("^~\\$", negate = TRUE)
length(questionnaire_files)

[1] 79


From the first processing step on, the questionnaires form one table, x, with one row per questionnaire; every processing step changes x and hands it to the next.
Which tools? The analysis of each step is written out. Only two summary tables and a figure that recur use small functions, defined once here:

Before and afterPersonsAgreement



# the questionnaires, persons and columns of the file at one point; persons
# are the codes in `code` (from 1.3) or the pseudonyms in `id` (from 1.7)
file_size <- \(data) {
  persons <- select(data, any_of(c("code", "id")))
  tibble(questionnaires = nrow(data),
         persons        = if (ncol(persons) == 1) n_distinct(persons) else NA,
         columns        = ncol(data))
}




# one line per person: the waves, ages and sexes of their questionnaires
describe_persons <- \(data, ids) {
  data |>
    filter(code %in% ids) |>
    summarise(waves = paste0("T", sort(unique(Occasion)), collapse = ", "),
              age   = paste(unique(age), collapse = "/"),
              sex   = paste(unique(sex), collapse = "/"),
              .by = code)
}




# the share of identical answers of two questionnaires against the number
# of different values in the earlier one: one person in March and in
# September (grey) beside the pairs examined (blue)
plot_agreement <- \(reference, cases, label) {
  reference_label <- "one person, March and September"
  bind_rows(mutate(reference, pair = reference_label),
            mutate(cases, pair = label)) |>
    mutate(pair = factor(pair, levels = c(reference_label, label))) |>
    ggplot(aes(values, identical, colour = pair)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 95, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = .8,
               position = position_jitter(width = .15, height = 0,
                                          seed = 1)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey65", "#2a78d6")) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
    labs(x = "different values in the earlier questionnaire",
         y = "identical answers (%)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
What stands between the files and one table? The municipality and the wave are not in the files, only in their names, and the names spell the municipalities in several ways (Arlje and Arilje, Sid and SID). The label rows and the empty rows are no questionnaires. Because the label rows are text, every column of every file is read as text, the answers included. The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
How are the files read? One function reads a file: the answers below the three label rows, the municipality and the wave from the file name, the empty rows dropped. All files are read in one fixed order and stacked; the notes are set aside:

# The questionnaires: one Excel file per municipality and wave
# -> one row per questionnaire

# one fixed order on every computer: where a code leaves age or sex blank at
# one wave, it is filled from the questionnaire read first
excel_files <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.xlsx$", full.names = TRUE) |>
  str_subset("/~\\$", negate = TRUE) |>   # not the lock files of open workbooks
  stri_sort(locale = "en_US")

if (length(excel_files) != 79) {
  stop("Expected the 79 Excel files in '", raw_dir, "', found ",
       length(excel_files), " (see data/README.md).", call. = FALSE)
}

# One file: the answers below three label rows (Serbian wording, an empty
# row, English wording), municipality and wave from the file name, e.g.
# "Arilje - Trainee Questionnaires - December 2025", empty rows dropped.
read_questionnaires <- \(file) {
  name  <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))
  month <- months_list[str_detect(name, regex(months_list, ignore_case = TRUE))]
  answers <- read_excel(file, .name_repair = "unique_quiet") |>
    mutate(across(where(is.character), enc2utf8)) |>
    slice(-(1:3)) |>
    mutate(Municipality = sub("Trainees.*", "", sub("^(.*?)-.*", "\\1", name)),
           Occasion     = month[1])
  answers[rowSums(is.na(answers)) < ncol(answers) - 2, ]
}

raw <- excel_files |>
  map(read_questionnaires) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(sex          = toupper(trimws(sex)),
         age          = as.numeric(age),
         Municipality = trimws(Municipality),
         Occasion     = trimws(Occasion))

# five files carry notes of the data entry in an unnamed extra column
entry_notes <- raw |>
  filter(!is.na(`...111`)) |>
  select(Municipality, Occasion, note = `...111`)

raw <- raw |> select(-`...111`)

Next → Step 2, the problem: What can go wrong with such a code?


Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
What can go wrong with such a code? The same code at two waves marks the same person, so a code typed differently at one wave makes one person look like two; a letter typed once with and once without its diacritic is such a difference. The code says nothing about the municipality, which has to come from the spelling of the file names. And age or sex is left blank on some questionnaires, though given at the person’s other waves.
Next → Step 3, the rule: How is the code built?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
How is the code built? One spelling per municipality, the waves numbered 0 to 3, the letter without its diacritic, the code from the first three columns completed by the first two letters of the municipality; age or sex left blank at one wave is taken from the same code’s other waves, and each municipality gets its condition:

# Municipalities, waves, participant codes, condition

x <- raw |>
  mutate(
    # municipality names as in the file names -> one spelling, with diacritics
    Municipality = gsub(" ", "", Municipality),
    Municipality = case_when(
      Municipality == "Arlje"                   ~ "Arilje",
      Municipality == "Bac"                     ~ "Bač",
      Municipality %in% c("Kanijza", "Kanjiza") ~ "Kanjiža",
      Municipality == "Uzice"                   ~ "Užice",
      Municipality == "Sabac"                   ~ "Šabac",
      Municipality == "Vrsac"                   ~ "Vršac",
      Municipality == "Pozarevac"               ~ "Požarevac",
      Municipality %in% c("SID", "Sid")         ~ "Šid",
      Municipality == "Krusevac"                ~ "Kruševac",
      Municipality == "Raska"                   ~ "Raška",
      TRUE                                      ~ Municipality
    ),
    Municipality = stri_trans_nfc(Municipality),   # one form for č, š, ž
    # wave: 0 = January (T0), 1 = March, 2 = September, 3 = December (T3)
    Occasion    = match(Occasion, months_list) - 1,
    `Month...2` = as.numeric(`Month...2`),
    `Day...3`   = as.numeric(`Day...3`),
    age         = as.numeric(age)
  )

# The participant code: third letter of the mother's first name, month and day
# of her birth, first two letters of the municipality, e.g. "M315Ar". The
# questionnaire asks for it twice, at the start (columns 1-3) and at the end
# (columns 108-110); the code is built from the first.
x <- x |>
  mutate(
    # Serbian letters with diacritics -> plain letters
    `Letter...1` = gsub("Ž", "Z", `Letter...1`),
    `Letter...1` = gsub("Š", "S", `Letter...1`),
    `Letter...1` = gsub("Đ", "D", `Letter...1`),
    muni_prefix  = stri_trans_general(Municipality, "Latin-ASCII") |>
                   substr(1, 2),
    code         = paste0(`Letter...1`, `Month...2`, `Day...3`, muni_prefix)
  )

x <- x |>
  # age or sex left blank at one wave -> from the same code's other waves
  group_by(code) |>
  fill(age, sex, .direction = "downup") |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(condition = if_else(Municipality %in% trained_first,
                             "Experimental", "Control"))

The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
Which codes were corrected before this report, and on what grounds? Codes that differ in one letter or digit (in three cases in two parts), within a municipality and with the same age and sex, were set to one spelling. The corrections were found in five rounds between December 2025 and February 2026. The two shared codes are first told apart by sex and age; the corrections are then applied in the order found, as some build on earlier ones:

# Mistyped codes, corrected in five rounds (December 2025 to February 2026):
# codes that differ in one letter or digit, within a municipality and with the
# same age and sex, are set to one spelling; `mistyped` names the part of the
# code that differed (the letter, the month or the day)

# two codes that stood for more than one person -> told apart by sex and age
x <- x |>
  mutate(code = case_when(

Next → Step 2, the problem: What do the five rounds not catch?


Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
What do the five rounds not catch? Three kinds of error. One person may still be under two codes, when the letter was written in another script or spelling (the Serbian Lj as one letter or two, a Cyrillic A for a Latin one), when the day was left blank, or when the code was written differently at two waves but the same way at the end of one questionnaire. Two people may be under one code, as after round 5. And one paper form may have been typed in twice, once for its own wave and once for the next, so that one answer sheet counts for two waves.

            end_day    = `Day...110`)

joins_evidence <- code_merges |>
  left_join(describe_persons(corr_before, code_merges$code_from),
            by = c(code_from = "code")) |>
  left_join(describe_persons(corr_before, code_merges$code_to),
            by = c(code_to = "code"), suffix = c("", "_joined")) |>
  left_join(corr_parts, by = c(code_from = "code")) |>
  left_join(select(corr_parts, code, letter_joined = letter,
                   month_joined = month, day_joined = day),
            by = c(code_to = "code")) |>
  mutate(
    # a part differs unless both are equal or both blank
    letter_differs = !coalesce(letter == letter_joined,
                               is.na(letter) & is.na(letter_joined)),
    month_differs  = !coalesce(month == month_joined,
                               is.na(month) & is.na(month_joined)),
    day_differs    = !coalesce(day == day_joined,
                               is.na(day) & is.na(day_joined)),
    parts_differ = pmap_chr(
      list(letter_differs, month_differs, day_differs),
      \(l, m, d) str_flatten(c("letter", "month", "day")[c(l, m, d)], " and ")
    ),
    # the code at the end: left blank, or that of the person joined?
    end_names_joined = case_when(
      is.na(end_letter) & is.na(end_month) & is.na(end_day) ~ "blank",
      coalesce(end_letter == letter_joined,
               is.na(end_letter) & is.na(letter_joined)) &
        coalesce(end_month == month_joined,
                 is.na(end_month) & is.na(month_joined)) &
        coalesce(end_day == day_joined,
                 is.na(end_day) & is.na(day_joined))      ~ "yes",
      TRUE                                                ~ "no"
    )
  )

Next → Step 5, before and after: How are the lists applied?



The result · Steps 5 and 6

Step 5 · Before and after all questionnaires
How are the lists applied? All three together, after checking that every listed questionnaire is there exactly as listed; case_log records each correction:

# The corrections of this report, applied after checking that every listed
# questionnaire is there exactly as listed; `case_log` records each one

# Stops with the listed codes that are not found exactly once; `listed`
# holds the columns that identify the questionnaire.
expect_once <- \(listed, what) {
  found   <- listed |> left_join(count(x, pick(all_of(names(listed)))),
                                 by = names(listed))
  missing <- found$code[is.na(found$n) | found$n != 1]
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop(what, ": not found exactly once: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
         call. = FALSE)
  }
}

# Stops naming the codes, if any.
stop_if_any <- \(codes, what) {
  if (length(codes) > 0) {
    stop(what, ": ", paste(unique(codes), collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
  }
}

# the join list: every code exists, none is listed twice, none is both
# joined and a join target (no chains)
stop_if_any(setdiff(c(code_merges$code_from, code_merges$code_to), x$code),
            "Join: no questionnaire with the code")
stop_if_any(code_merges$code_from[duplicated(code_merges$code_from)],
            "Join: listed twice")
stop_if_any(intersect(code_merges$code_from, code_merges$code_to),
            "Join: joined and also a join target")

# a join must not give a person two questionnaires at one wave
clashes <- code_merges |>
  inner_join(distinct(x, code, Occasion), by = c(code_from = "code")) |>
  inner_join(distinct(x, code, Occasion), by = c(code_to = "code", "Occasion"))
stop_if_any(clashes$code_from,
            "Join: a questionnaire at the same wave as its join target")

expect_once(select(code_splits, code, Occasion, age), "Split")
expect_once(select(double_entries, code, Occasion), "Double entry")

# waves as T0 to T3; the waves of each code that a join replaces (for the log)
wave <- \(occasion) paste0("T", occasion)
joined_waves <- x |>
  filter(code %in% code_merges$code_from) |>
  summarise(wave = paste(wave(sort(unique(Occasion))), collapse = ", "),
            .by = code)

# codes that already have more than one questionnaire at a wave (copies of
# one form, see 1.5): joins and splits must not add to them, e.g. by joining
# two codes onto one
repeated_before <- x |> count(code, Occasion) |> filter(n > 1)

x <- x |>
  # one person, two codes -> one code
  left_join(select(code_merges, code = code_from, code_to), by = "code") |>
  mutate(code = coalesce(code_to, code)) |>
  select(-code_to) |>
  # two people, one code -> the second gets its own code back
  left_join(code_splits, by = c("code", "Occasion", "age")) |>
  mutate(code = coalesce(new_code, code)) |>
  select(-new_code)

repeated_after <- x |> count(code, Occasion) |> filter(n > 1)
new_repeats    <- repeated_after |>
  anti_join(repeated_before, by = c("code", "Occasion"))
stop_if_any(new_repeats$code, "Join: two questionnaires at one wave for")

# one form, entered twice -> the later entry removed
n_before <- nrow(x)
x <- x |> anti_join(double_entries, by = c("code", "Occasion"))
if (n_before - nrow(x) != nrow(double_entries)) {
  stop("Double entry: removed ", n_before - nrow(x), " entries, listed ",
       nrow(double_entries), call. = FALSE)
}

case_log <- bind_rows(
  code_merges |>
    left_join(joined_waves, by = c(code_from = "code")) |>
    transmute(correction = "codes joined", code = code_from, wave,
              change = paste("now", code_to)),
  code_splits |>
    transmute(correction = "code split", code, wave = wave(Occasion),
              change = paste("one questionnaire now", new_code)),
  double_entries |>
    transmute(correction = "double entry removed", code, wave = wave(Occasion),
              change = paste("same form as", same_form_as_code,
                             wave(same_form_as_occasion)))
)

Next → Step 6, what follows: Where do the corrections go from here?


Step 6 · What follows
Where do the corrections go from here? The case log is completed in 1.6 and leaves the chapter with the file (1.7). Chapter 4 searches all pairs of questionnaires once more for forms entered twice (4.9); the sample set without them (S7, Chapter 3) equals the full sample, as they are removed here.

Next → Step 2, the problem: What cannot be scored as it stands?


Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
What cannot be scored as it stands? Text: “7 or 8” names two answers, “/” and “no answ.” none. Some numbers carry an extra digit, such as 1010 where the scale ends at 10. And the files cut the last letter of one item name (IntellectualCapita for IntellectualCapital).
Next → Step 3, the rule: What becomes of these entries?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
What becomes of these entries? Three answers typed with extra digits are set to the value meant; then every entry that is not one number becomes missing. An entry such as “7 or 8” is not split, as 7.5, say: the questionnaire asks for one answer.

# Item answers

x <- x |>
  mutate(

    Resonance1            = as.numeric(Resonance1) |>
                            rec(rules = "1010=10; else=copy"),
    IntellectualHumility6 = as.numeric(IntellectualHumility6) |>
                            rec(rules = "100=10; else=copy"),
    needSatisfaction21    = as.numeric(needSatisfaction21) |>
                            rec(rules = "99=9; else=copy")
  ) |>
  # the files cut the last letter of this item name
  rename_with(\(name) sub("IntellectualCapita", "IntellectualCapital", name)) |>
  # the 102 items; entries that are not one number ("7 or 8", "no answ.")
  # -> missing
  mutate(across(ListenOther1:needSatisfaction24,
                \(answer) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(answer))))

section: 2.1 How each processing step is examined
text:
2.1 How each processing step is examined
What happens at each processing step? The same six steps as in Chapter 1, in three parts and always in the same order: the problem, the rule and the result. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph PROBLEM["the problem"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>what the data look like"] --> S2{{"<b>Step 2</b><br>the problem:<br>what could the analyses<br>not use?"}}
  end
  subgraph RULE["the rule"]
    direction LR
    S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>the rule,<br>one code file"] --> S4["<b>Step 4</b><br>the evidence<br>per case"]
  end
  subgraph RESULT["the result"]
    direction LR
    S5["<b>Step 5</b><br>before and after"] --> S6["<b>Step 6</b><br>what follows"]
  end
  PROBLEM --> RULE
  RULE --> RESULT
  classDef all fill:#efeff2,stroke:#8a8a8a,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f
  class S1,S2,S3,S4,S5 all
  class S6 verdict
  style PROBLEM fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style RULE fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style RESULT fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a






The six steps in detail:
The problem:

What the data look like. The dataset as the processing step finds it: the items, answers or columns it is about. The step keeps a copy of this dataset (…_before) where Step 5 compares.
The problem. What the later analyses could not use, or would misread, if the data stayed as they are.

The rule:

The rule. The change, written once in a code file of its own (R/ch02_….R, R/scales.R) and applied to every questionnaire alike.
The evidence per case. Every item, scale or person the rule touches, with the data it rests on. An item counts as reverse-keyed if a high answer means less of its construct, by its wording. A score is the mean of its items if at least one is answered. An item that is answered almost always at the top of the scale in January (a mean above 9.7) cannot show a change and leaves the score.

The result:

Before and after. The rows, persons and columns of the dataset before and after the processing step, and what changed for the cases of Step 4.
What follows. Which chapters use the result, and for what.

Next → Step 2, the problem: Which items point the other way?


Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
Which items point the other way? Every item is answered from 0 to 10. For 22 items a high answer means less of the construct, such as “I feel excluded from the group I want to belong to” for relatedness; averaged with the other items as they stand, they would cancel them out. The names of the need-satisfaction items do not say which subscale they belong to. And the wave, the condition and sex are stored as numbers or as text that the models cannot order.
Next → Step 3, the rule: What changes?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
What changes? The 22 reverse-keyed items are turned around (10 − x), so that high always means more; the need-satisfaction items are named by their subscales, and alienation and isolation by what a high answer now means (no alienation, no isolation); the wave, the condition and sex become factors with their labels:

# Items: reverse-keyed items turned around, the need-satisfaction block named
# by its six subscales, and the design columns as factors

# the 22 reverse-keyed items: 10 - x on the scale from 0 to 10
reverse_items <- c(
  "Alienation1", "Alienation2", "Isolation1", "Isolation2",
  "Flourishing5", "Flourishing6",
  "Rogerian7", "Rogerian8", "Rogerian9",
  "ToleranceDiversity1",
  paste0("needSatisfaction", seq(2, 24, by = 2))
)

# old name = new name; the 24 need-satisfaction items rotate through the six
# subscales (item 1 autonomy satisfaction, 2 autonomy non-frustration, ...,
# 7 autonomy satisfaction again)
need <- \(numbers) paste0("needSatisfaction", numbers)
rename_map <- c(
  "Alienation1" = "NoAlienation1", "Alienation2" = "NoAlienation2",
  "Isolation1"  = "NoIsolation1",  "Isolation2"  = "NoIsolation2",
  set_names(paste0("AutonomySatisfaction",     1:4), need(c(1, 7, 13, 19))),
  set_names(paste0("AutonomyNonFrustrated",    1:4), need(c(2, 8, 14, 20))),
  set_names(paste0("RelatednessSatisfaction",  1:4), need(c(3, 9, 15, 21))),
  set_names(paste0("RelatednessNonFrustrated", 1:4), need(c(4, 10, 16, 22))),
  set_names(paste0("CompetenceSatisfaction",   1:4), need(c(5, 11, 17, 23))),
  set_names(paste0("CompetenceNonFrustrated",  1:4), need(c(6, 12, 18, 24)))
)

df <- x |>
  mutate(across(all_of(reverse_items), \(answer) 10 - answer)) |>
  rename_with(\(old) rename_map[old], all_of(names(rename_map))) |>
  mutate(
    Occasion  = factor(Occasion, levels = 0:3, labels = paste0("T", 0:3)),
    # Control first: group 1 in the multi-group models
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("Control", "Experimental")),
    # "NO ANSW." and "." -> missing
    sex       = case_match(sex, "F" ~ "Female", "M" ~ "Male")
  )

# the 102 items, from the first listening to the last need-satisfaction item
item_names <- names(select(df, ListenOther1:CompetenceNonFrustrated4))

Next → Step 2, the problem: How is a scale scored with blank answers?


Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
How is a scale scored with blank answers? A score that required every item would lose every questionnaire with one blank answer. And a composite of a hypothesis block can weigh each scale equally, as the mean of the scale scores, or each item, as the mean of all items of the block.
Next → Step 3, the rule: How is a scale scored?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
How is a scale scored? As the mean of its items, if at least one is answered. The three hypothesis composites pool all items of their block into one mean, rather than averaging the scale scores, so that a scale with more items weighs more.

# Scale scores: the mean of a scale's items (at least one answered); the
# women's attitude score also with all nine items; and the three hypothesis
# composites, the mean of the pooled items of their block

  map(\(items) row_means(df[setdiff(items, ceiling_items)], min_valid = 1))

composites <- list(H1_ListeningTogetherness = h1_items,
                   H2_CognitiveComplexity   = h2_items,
                   H3_Wellbeing             = h3_items) |>
  map(\(items) row_means(df[items], min_valid = 1))

df <- df |>
  bind_cols(scores) |>
  mutate(womenAttitude_full = row_means(pick(all_of(scale_items$womenAttitude)),
                                        min_valid = 1),
         .after = womenAttitude) |>
  bind_cols(composites)

Next → Step 2, the problem: How do the models know who was trained when?


Step 2 · The problem all questionnaires
How do the models know who was trained when? The multilevel models of Chapter 10 need the trainer of each municipality, as the trainings of one trainer may resemble each other, and codings of time that mark when each group was trained.
Next → Step 3, the rule: What is added?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all questionnaires
What is added? Each municipality had one of ten trainers; each trainer trained one municipality of each condition. The codings of time and training follow from the condition and the wave:

# Design variables: the trainer of each municipality (each trainer trained
# one municipality of each condition) and the codings of time and training
# that the multilevel models use (Chapter 10)

trainers <- tribble(
  ~trainer, ~trained_first, ~trained_second,
  1,        "Kula",         "Vršac",
  2,        "Valjevo",      "Bač",
  3,        "Sokobanja",    "Prijepolje",
  4,        "Leskovac",     "Arilje",
  5,        "Kruševac",     "Pirot",
  6,        "Šid",          "Požarevac",
  7,        "Raška",        "Šabac",
  8,        "NoviPazar",    "Lebane",
  9,        "Užice",        "Kikinda",
  10,       "Kanjiža",      "Vlasotince"
)

trainer_of <- trainers |>
  pivot_longer(c(trained_first, trained_second), values_to = "Municipality") |>
  transmute(Municipality, trainedBy = factor(trainer))

df <- df |>
  left_join(trainer_of, by = "Municipality") |>
  mutate(
    # 1 once the person's own group is trained: experimental from T1,
    # control at T3
    D = as.integer((condition == "Experimental" & Occasion != "T0") |
                   (condition == "Control"      & Occasion == "T3")),
    # piecewise time: the first training (from T1), the second training (T3)
    Time_Exp_Training     = ifelse(Occasion == "T0", 0, 1),
    Time_Control_Training = ifelse(Occasion == "T3", 1, 0),
    # Helmert contrasts: T0 against the later waves, T3 against the earlier
    TF_helmert = ifelse(Occasion == "T0", -3, 1),
    TS_helmert = ifelse(Occasion == "T3",  3, -1)
  )

What do the latent and the mediation models need? One row per person, with every wave’s answers side by side. Age and sex, however, are given on every questionnaire and need not agree between a person’s waves.
Next → Step 3, the rule: How are the waves put side by side?



The rule · Steps 3 and 4

Step 3 · The rule all persons
How are the waves put side by side? The items and the composites of each wave in columns of their own, and for each person one age (the mean of the ages given) and one sex (the one given most often):

# One row per person: the items of every wave side by side (ListenOther1_T0,
# ...), age, sex and attendance, the centred covariates of the structured
# means models (Chapter 11), the composites per wave for the mediation models
# (Chapter 12), and one dummy per training round

# sex: the answer given most often (one person gave F and M once each; the
# tie goes to "Female", the first in alphabetical order)
modal_sex <- df |>
  drop_na(sex) |>
  count(id, sex) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 1, by = id, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  select(id, sex)

person <- df |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(age     = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_waves = n_distinct(Occasion),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(modal_sex, by = "id") |>
  mutate(age_c  = age - mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),   # centred at the mean
         female = case_match(sex, "Female" ~ 1, "Male" ~ 0))

df_wide <- df |>
  filter(!is.na(condition)) |>
  select(id, condition, Occasion, all_of(item_names)) |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols     = c(id, condition),
              names_from  = Occasion,
              values_from = all_of(item_names),
              names_glue  = "{.value}_{Occasion}") |>
  left_join(person, by = "id") |>
  left_join(distinct(df, id, Municipality), by = "id")

# the three composites per wave, named as the mediation models expect
mediation_composites <- df |>
  select(id, Occasion,
         Hypothesis1_ListeningTogetherness = H1_ListeningTogetherness,
         Hypothesis2_CognitiveComplexity   = H2_CognitiveComplexity,
         Hypothesis3_Wellbeing             = H3_Wellbeing) |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols     = id,
              names_from  = Occasion,
              names_glue  = "{Occasion}_{.value}",
              values_from = starts_with("Hypothesis"))

df_wide <- df_wide |>
  left_join(mediation_composites, by = "id") |>
  mutate(train_eg = ifelse(condition == "Experimental", 1, 0),  # trained T0-T1
         train_cg = ifelse(condition == "Control", 1, 0))       # trained T2-T3

title: 18. Final structure
text:
18.1 How each analysis is examined
Which analyses? Seven, in the order of the pipeline. The first two repeat the network analyses of Chapter 16 on the final pool of Chapter 17: the hierarchical structure of the items at each wave, and its bootstrap at T0. The next three turn the communities into composite scores and ask how these group into factors, at T0 and at each wave. The last two describe the items and composites by item response models: the information of every item, and the reliability of every composite.
What happens in each analysis? The same six steps, in the same order and in three parts: the analysis, its result, and what follows. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph P0["the analysis"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>the starting point"]
    S1 --> S2["<b>Step 2</b><br>the method and<br>the criterion"]
    S2 --> S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>the estimation"]
  end
  subgraph P1["the result"]
    direction LR
    S4{{"<b>Step 4</b><br>the result"}}
    S4 --> S5["<b>Step 5</b><br>where it strains"]
  end
  V["<b>Step 6</b><br>what follows"]
  P0 --> P1
  P1 --> V
  classDef all fill:#efeff2,stroke:#8a8a8a,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f
  class S1,S2,S3,S4,S5 all
  class V verdict
  style P0 fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style P1 fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a






The six steps in detail:
The analysis:

The starting point. Which items or composites enter, from which questionnaires.
The method and the criterion. How the analysis works, with its settings, and by which criterion it judges its result. As in Chapter 16: an item’s stability is the share of 500 bootstrap samples in which it lands in its community or its factor; a community or a factor is structurally consistent when it reappears with exactly the same items in at least 75 % of the samples; two partitions of the same items are compared by the share of item pairs they treat alike (the Rand index, 1 when they are the same); TEFI compares solutions on the same items, lower is better. A graded response model (GRM) needs at least three items, as in Chapter 17. The decisions taken in a step, such as the names of the composites and factors, are stated here with their reason.
The estimation. The code. The bootstraps take a few minutes each and run in the pipeline script of Chapters 16 to 18; this chapter reads their results. The hierarchical solutions at each wave, the composite scores and the item response models are estimated here.

The result:

The result. What the analysis finds, with a figure where it shows something.
Where it strains. Where the result is weakest: the waves, items or composites on which it rests least firmly.

What follows:

What follows. Where the result goes next.

Next → Step 2, the method and the criterion: How is the structure found, and how are two waves compared?


Step 2 · The method and the criterion each wave
How is the structure found, and how are two waves compared? As in Chapter 16.3: hierEGA groups the items into communities (lower order), scores each person on each community from the network, and groups the community scores into factors (higher order). Louvain visits the items in random order, so each wave gets the seed it has in Chapter 16. TEFI compares solutions on the same items; a later wave is compared with T0 by the Rand index over all pairs of items.
Next → Step 3, the estimation: How is it run?


Step 3 · The estimation each wave
How is it run? hierEGA once per wave, each wave with its seed:

final_seeds <- c(T0 = 123, T1 = 456, T2 = 789, T3 = 101112)

hier <- map2(final_answers, final_seeds, \(answers, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  hierEGA(answers, scores = "network", loading.method = "revised",
          corr = "auto", na.data = "pairwise", model = "glasso",
          plot.EGA = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
})

The number of communities and factors at each wave, the community and factor of every item, and the T0 solution in the order of its factors and communities:

hier_sizes <- hier |>
  map(\(h) tibble(lower  = h$lower_order$n.dim,
                  higher = h$higher_order$n.dim,
                  TEFI   = h$TEFI)) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "wave")

hier_by_wave <- hier |>
  map(\(h) h$dim.variables |>
        as_tibble() |>
        transmute(item = items, lower = as.integer(lower),
                  higher = as.integer(higher))) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "wave")

assignment <- hier_by_wave |>
  filter(wave == "T0") |>
  select(-wave) |>
  arrange(higher, lower, item)

Next → Step 2, the method and the criterion: How is a composite scored and named?


Step 2 · The method and the criterion January
How is a composite scored and named? A composite is the mean of a person’s answered items of a community. It takes the short name of its scale (community_name() in the tab Composite functions); a community that mixes scales is called Connection, since it gathers listening, being moved and feeling understood. Its reliability is Cronbach’s α on the questionnaires that answer all its items.
Next → Step 3, the estimation: How is it computed?


Step 3 · The estimation January
How is it computed? The items of each composite, in the order of the communities, and each composite with its items, α and mean at T0:

composites <- assignment |>
  arrange(lower) |>
  mutate(composite = community_name(item), .by = lower) |>
  mutate(composite = fct_inorder(composite))

  summarise(community = first(lower),
            items     = str_flatten_comma(item),
            k         = n(),
            alpha     = cronbach(items_T0[item]),
            mean_T0   = mean(rowMeans(items_T0[item], na.rm = TRUE),
                             na.rm = TRUE),

Next → Step 2, the method and the criterion: How do the composites group?


Step 2 · The method and the criterion January
How do the composites group? EGA of the composite scores (graphical lasso, walktrap), bootstrapped on 500 parametric samples with seed 42 (boot_ega() in the tab Network functions). A composite’s stability is the share of samples in which it lands in the same dimension as in the observed data. A dimension is named after its composites (factor_name()): one that holds Connection is called Engagement, one that holds Flourishing Well-being and agency.
Next → Step 3, the estimation: How does the script run it?


Step 3 · The estimation January
How does the script run it? One bootstrap per wave, of which this analysis reads T0:

boot_wave <- \(wave) boot_ega(composite_scores(df, composites, wave))
composite_boot <- tibble(wave = names(hier_seeds)) |>
  mutate(boot        = map(wave, boot_wave),
         n           = map_int(boot, \(b) b$EGA$n),
         dimensions  = map_int(boot, \(b) b$EGA$n.dim),
         stability   = map(boot, item_stability),
         consistency = map(boot, structural_consistency),
         frequency   = map(boot, \(b) as_tibble(b$frequency))) |>
  select(-boot)


composite_boot <- final$composite_boot
composite_T0 <- composite_boot |>
  filter(wave == "T0") |>
  pull(stability) |>
  pluck(1) |>
  rename(composite = item, dimension = community) |>

Next → Step 2, the method and the criterion: How good is each item?


Step 2 · The method and the criterion January
How good is each item? A GRM per composite with at least three items (as in Chapter 17) gives each item its discrimination a and its Fisher information I(θ) at three trait levels: θ = −2, 0 and +2, about two standard deviations below the mean, the mean, and two above. The item-rest correlation is the correlation of the item with the mean of the other items of its composite. A composite of two items has no GRM.
Next → Step 3, the estimation: How is each model fitted?


Step 3 · The estimation January
How is each model fitted? One GRM per composite, with the discrimination, the information at the three trait levels and the marginal reliability:

theta_levels <- c(-2, 0, 2)

grm <- composites |>
  filter(n() >= 3, .by = composite) |>
  summarise(items = list(item), .by = composite) |>
  mutate(fit = map(items, \(i)
    mirt(drop_na(items_T0[i]), 1, itemtype = "graded", verbose = FALSE)),
    reliability = map_dbl(fit, marginal_rxx),
    a = map(fit, \(f)
      coef(f, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items |>
        as_tibble(rownames = "item") |>
        select(item, a)),
    information = map2(fit, items, \(f, i)
      map(seq_along(i), \(j)
        tibble(item = i[j], theta = theta_levels,
               information = iteminfo(extract.item(f, j),
                                      Theta = matrix(theta_levels)))) |>
        list_rbind()))

master <- composites |>
  arrange(higher, lower) |>
  left_join(select(factors, composite, factor), by = "composite") |>
  mutate(item_rest = item_rest(items_T0[item]), .by = composite) |>

              pivot_wider(names_from = theta, values_from = information,
                          names_prefix = "I_"),
            by = "item") |>
  select(factor, composite, item, a, `I_-2`, I_0, I_2, item_rest)

section: 19.1 How each factor and each window is examined
text:
19.1 How each factor and each window is examined
What happens to each factor? The two factors of Chapter 18 and the single item on life satisfaction go through the same six steps, in the same order and in four parts: the score, the effect, the measurement, and what follows. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph P0["the score"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>the score"]
    S1 --> S2["<b>Step 2</b><br>means by condition<br>and wave"]
  end
  subgraph P1["the effect: both groups"]
    direction LR
    S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>Δd in the two<br>training windows"]
    S3 --> S4["<b>Step 4</b><br>the multilevel<br>model"]
  end
  subgraph P2["the measurement"]
    direction LR
    S5{{"<b>Step 5</b><br>the same measurement<br>over the waves"}}
  end

  P2 --> V

The six steps in detail:
The score:

The score. The communities and items of the factor (Chapter 18). A person’s factor score is the mean of the items they answered, and so is each community score. How consistent the score is: Cronbach’s α over the factor’s items at each wave, on the questionnaires that answer them all.
Means by condition and wave. The mean and standard deviation of the score in each group at each wave, over all questionnaires of that wave, and a figure of their course: the bars span one standard error of the mean (SD / √n) on either side, the training of the experimental group (T0 to T1) is shaded orange, that of the control group (T2 to T3) blue, as in Chapter 9.

The effect:

Δd in the two training windows. The repeated-measures Δd of Chapter 9, for the factor score and for each of its community scores: the d of the experimental group minus the d of the control group, each the mean change of the persons who answered at both waves divided by their standard deviation at the first wave, with a two-sided z-test, significant at p < .05. While the experimental group trains (T0 to T1), a positive Δd means that it gains more; while the control group trains (T2 to T3), a negative Δd means that the control group gains more. The effect of the factor is set beside those of the preregistered composites in the same window (Chapter 9).
The multilevel model. The preregistered model of Chapter 10, outcome ~ Occasion * condition + (1 | Municipality/id), fitted by REML and tested with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Each interaction term OccasionTk:conditionExperimental compares the change from T0 to wave k between the groups (positive: the experimental group changes more), tested two-sided at α = .05.

The measurement:

The same measurement over the waves. A latent difference-in-differences (Chapter 11) compares latent means, and that needs scalar invariance over the waves (Chapter 7). Each factor gets the longitudinal model of Chapter 7, with its community scores as indicators: one factor per wave, the first community as the marker, the four factors correlated, and each community’s residual correlated with itself over the waves, fitted by robust maximum likelihood with missing waves by full information. The configural model needs a robust CFI of at least .90. The metric model holds the loadings equal over the waves, the scalar model the intercepts as well; a level holds when, against the level before, the robust CFI drops by no more than .010 and the robust RMSEA rises by no more than .015 (Chen, 2007; the cutoffs of Chapter 7 for samples of more than 300). A single item has no measurement model, so life satisfaction skips this step.

What follows:

What follows. Where the results go next.

What happens in each window of the pathway? The question is whether the training reaches well-being through engagement. In each of the four windows of Chapter 12, Engagement at the end of the window is regressed on the training, and Well-being and agency on Engagement and the training; both regressions control for the two scores at the start of the window. Within a wave both scores are measured at the same time, so their order is an assumption of the model, as in Chapter 12. Each window goes through the same five steps, in three parts: the model, the effects, and what follows:





flowchart TB
  subgraph P0["the model"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>the model"]
    S1 --> S2{{"<b>Step 2</b><br>the path diagram:<br>does it fit?"}}
  end
  subgraph P1["the effects"]
    direction LR
    S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>the paths<br>and effects"]
    S3 --> S4["<b>Step 4</b><br>against the<br>preregistered pathway"]
  end
  V["<b>Step 5</b><br>what follows"]
  P0 --> P1
  P1 --> V
  classDef all fill:#efeff2,stroke:#8a8a8a,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f
  class S1,S2,S3,S4 all
  class V verdict
  style P0 fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style P1 fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a






The model:

The model. Its lavaan syntax, written out: the paths a (training → Engagement), b (Engagement → Well-being and agency) and c (training → Well-being and agency), and the indirect (a × b), direct (c) and total effects defined from them. Each model is fitted by maximum likelihood with 1,000 bootstrap draws and missing values by full information (FIML), as in Chapter 12.
The path diagram. The three paths, standardized, with stars for p < .05, .01 and .001, and the fit of the model. The model keeps two degrees of freedom: it takes the training to be unrelated to the two scores at the start of the window. Where this holds, the model fits closely (χ² test with p above .05, CFI from .95, SRMR below .08).

The effects:

The paths and effects. Unstandardized, with bias-corrected bootstrap intervals (95 %) and the p-value of the z-test. An effect carries when its interval excludes 0. An indirect effect that carries while the direct path does not is an indirect-only mediation; when both carry in the same direction, the mediation is complementary (Zhao et al., 2010).
Against the preregistered pathway. The standardized indirect, direct and total effects on well-being, next to those of Chapter 12, where the training reaches the preregistered well-being composite (H3) through H1 and H2 (FIML in both).

What follows:

What follows. Where the results of the window go next.

title: 19. Training effects on the new structure
text:
19.2 Data and tools
How are the new scores built? By the functions of R/new_structure.R: the map from each item to its community and factor (Chapter 18), the scores, the scores of each person side by side, the model of a window of the pathway, and the longitudinal model of a factor. The four windows of the pathway, with 1,000 bootstrap draws each, take about four minutes and run in a script of their own; the chapter reads their fits.

Scores and modelsMediation script



# Scores of the post hoc structure (Chapter 19): the two factors and the
# ten communities of Chapter 18, each the mean of a person's answered items.
# Needs R/structure_composites.R (composite_items(), factor_name()).

# item -> community (composite) -> factor, from the final structure
structure_map <- readRDS("cache/structure_final.rds")$assignment |>
  composite_items() |>
  mutate(factor = factor_name(unique(composite)), .by = higher) |>
  # column names without spaces: engagement, wellbeing_agency
  mutate(factor_score = if_else(factor == "Engagement", "engagement",
                                "wellbeing_agency"))

# the mean of the answered items, missing when none was answered
item_mean <- \(data, items) {
  m <- rowMeans(data[items], na.rm = TRUE)
  if_else(is.nan(m), NA, m)
}

# add the two factor scores and the ten composites (prefix new_)
add_new_scores <- \(data) {
  factors    <- split(structure_map$item, structure_map$factor_score)
  composites <- split(structure_map$item,
                      str_c("new_", structure_map$composite))
  data |>
    bind_cols(map(c(factors, composites), \(items) item_mean(data, items)) |>
                as_tibble())
}

# one row per person: the two factor scores at each wave, and the training
# indicators of Chapter 2
new_scores_wide <- \(data, wide) {
  data |>
    select(id, Occasion, engagement, wellbeing_agency) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = Occasion,
                values_from = c(engagement, wellbeing_agency)) |>
    left_join(select(wide, id, condition, train_eg, train_cg), by = "id")
}

# training -> engagement -> well-being and agency in one window, controlling
# for both scores at the start of the window
factor_mediation_model <- \(pre, post, treated) {
  before <- str_c(c("engagement_", "wellbeing_agency_"), pre)
  after  <- str_c(c("engagement_", "wellbeing_agency_"), post)
  controls <- str_c(before, collapse = " + ")
  c(str_c(after[1], " ~ a*", treated, " + ", controls),
    str_c(after[2], " ~ b*", after[1], " + c*", treated, " + ", controls),
    str_c(before[1], " ~~ ", before[2]),
    "indirect := a*b",
    "direct := c",
    "total := c + a*b") |>
    str_c(collapse = "\n")
}

# Measurement invariance of the two factors over the waves (19.3). Needs
# R/longitudinal_models.R (waves, at(), wave_pairs).

# the community scores that measure a factor, in the order of Chapter 18
indicators_of <- \(f) {
  communities <- structure_map |>
    filter(factor_score == f) |>
    distinct(composite) |>
    arrange(composite)
  str_c("new_", communities$composite)
}

# one row per person, in the order of `wide`: the ten community scores at
# each wave (new_Connection_T0, ...)
community_scores_wide <- \(data, wide) {
  scores <- data |>
    select(id, Occasion, starts_with("new_")) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = Occasion, values_from = starts_with("new_"),
                names_glue = "{.value}_{Occasion}")
  wide |>
    select(id) |>
    left_join(scores, by = "id")
}

# one factor per wave, its community scores as indicators (the first is
# the marker) and each score's residual correlated with itself over the
# waves; configural, metric (equal loadings) or scalar (equal intercepts,
# latent means free from T1 on), as in Chapter 7
factor_invariance_model <- \(f, level = c("configural", "metric",
                                          "scalar")) {
  level      <- match.arg(level)
  indicators <- indicators_of(f)
  labels <- if (level == "configural") rep("", length(indicators)) else
    str_c("lam", seq_along(indicators), "*")
  labels[1] <- "1*"
  loadings <- map_chr(waves, \(w) str_c(
    "F_", w, " =~ ", str_c(labels, at(indicators, w), collapse = " + ")))
  covariances <- map_chr(wave_pairs, \(p) str_c("F_", p[1], " ~~ F_", p[2]))
  means <- if (level == "scalar") {
    c("F_T0 ~ 0*1", str_c("F_", waves[-1], " ~ 1"))
  } else {
    str_c("F_", waves, " ~ 0*1")
  }
  intercepts <- if (level == "scalar") {
    imap(indicators, \(x, j) str_c(at(x, waves), " ~ tau", j, "*1")) |>
      unlist()
  } else {
    character()
  }
  across_waves <- map(indicators, \(x) map_chr(wave_pairs, \(p)
    str_c(at(x, p[1]), " ~~ ", at(x, p[2])))) |> unlist()
  c(loadings, covariances, means, intercepts, across_waves) |>
    str_c(collapse = "\n")
}




# Mediation on the post hoc structure (Chapter 19): training -> engagement
# -> well-being and agency, in the four windows of Chapter 12, 1,000
# bootstrap draws each (about 4 minutes)
# Run from swt-website/ after Chapter 18:
#   Rscript scripts/new_structure_mediation.R

source("R/packages.R")
source("R/settings.R")
source("R/structure_composites.R")
source("R/new_structure.R")
source("R/mediation_model.R")           # windows, fit_mediation() (Ch. 12)
df      <- readRDS("cache/df.rds") |> add_new_scores()
df_wide <- readRDS("cache/df_wide.rds")
wide    <- new_scores_wide(df, df_wide)

new_mediation <- mediation_windows |>
  mutate(window = str_c(pre, " to ", post),
         syntax = pmap_chr(list(pre, post, treated), factor_mediation_model),
         fit    = map(syntax, \(m) fit_mediation(m, wide))) |>
  relocate(window, .after = model)

saveRDS(new_mediation, "cache/new_structure_mediation.rds")




Which data? All questionnaires with the new scores added (the two factor scores engagement and wellbeing_agency, the ten community scores with the prefix new_), the community scores of each person at the four waves side by side for the longitudinal models (Step 5), the fits of the four windows of the pathway, and for comparison the Δd of the preregistered composites (Chapter 9) and their effects on well-being in the preregistered pathway (Chapter 12):

df               <- add_new_scores(df)
communities_wide <- community_scores_wide(df, df_wide)
new_mediation    <- readRDS("cache/new_structure_mediation.rds")

# Chapter 9: Δd of the three preregistered composites
preregistered_d <- readRDS("cache/means.rds")$effects |>
  filter(outcome %in% c("H1_ListeningTogetherness",
                        "H2_CognitiveComplexity", "H3_Wellbeing"))

# Chapter 12: effects on H3, under the names of this chapter's model
preregistered <- readRDS("cache/mediation.rds")$estimators |>
  filter(estimator == "fiml",
         label %in% c("total_indirect", "directH3", "totalH3")) |>
  transmute(model,
            effect = c(total_indirect = "indirect", directH3 = "direct",
                       totalH3 = "total")[label],
            beta_chapter12 = beta, p_chapter12 = p)

The fits of the pathway include all 451 persons; those without any answer in a window carry no information on it.
Which tools? The analysis of each step is written out for every factor and every window. Only the figures and the fit table of the longitudinal models use small functions, defined once here:

TrajectoryLoadings over the wavesFitPath diagram



# the means of both groups at the four waves, with one standard error on
# either side; the two training periods shaded in the colour of the group
plot_trajectory <- \(means) {
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = .3)     # the two groups side by side
  means |>
    mutate(se = SD / sqrt(n)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = Occasion, y = M, colour = condition, shape = condition,
               group = condition)) +
    scale_x_discrete() +
    annotate("rect", xmin = 1, xmax = 2, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
             fill = "#eb6834", alpha = .08) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = 3, xmax = 4, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
             fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = .08) +
    geom_linerange(aes(ymin = M - se, ymax = M + se), linewidth = .5,
                   position = dodge) +
    geom_line(linewidth = .7, position = dodge) +
    geom_point(size = 2.2, position = dodge) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(Control = "#2a78d6",
                                   Experimental = "#eb6834")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean (0 to 10)", colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}




# the standardized loading of each community score at each wave, from
# one longitudinal model
wave_colours <- c(T0 = "#2a78d6", T1 = "#eb6834", T2 = "#1baf7a",
                  T3 = "#eda100")
plot_loadings_waves <- \(fit) {
  standardizedSolution(fit) |>
    filter(op == "=~") |>
    mutate(wave      = str_remove(lhs, "^F_"),
           community = str_remove(rhs, "_T[0-3]$") |> str_remove("^new_")) |>
    ggplot(aes(wave, est.std, group = community)) +
    geom_line(colour = "grey70", linewidth = .6) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = wave), size = 2.6) +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = \(d) filter(d, wave == "T3"),
                             aes(label = community), direction = "y",
                             nudge_x = .15, hjust = 0, size = 3.3,
                             segment.colour = "grey80") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = wave_colours, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(.3, 1.6))) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "standardized loading") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}




# the fit of a longitudinal model in one row
fit_indices <- \(fit) {
  fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq.scaled", "df", "cfi.robust", "rmsea.robust",
                     "srmr")) |>
    as.list() |>
    as_tibble() |>
    set_names(c("chisq", "df", "CFI", "RMSEA", "SRMR"))
}




# the fit beside the diagram, and its title above
fit_text <- \(fit, title = "") {
  values <- fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "tli",
                               "rmsea", "srmr"))
  labels <- c("ChiSq", "df", "p", "CFI", "TLI", "RMSEA", "SRMR")
  text(1.15, -.4, labels = str_c(labels, " = ", round(values, 3),
                                 collapse = "\n"),
       pos = 4, cex = .75)
  text(0, 1.4, labels = title, cex = 1)
}

# the three paths of a window as a path diagram: the training, and the
# two scores at the end of the window (the scores at its start, which both
# regressions control for, are left out); standardized estimates, stars
# for their significance
mediationPlot <- \(fit, title) {
  ends     <- lavNames(fit, "eqs.y")  # the two scores at the end
  training <- lavNames(fit, "ov.x")   # train_eg or train_cg
  starts   <- setdiff(lavNames(fit, "ov"), c(ends, training))
  wave     <- str_sub(ends[1], -2)
  semPlotModel(fit) |>
    drop_nodes(starts) |>
    semPaths(whatLabels = "std", style = "mx",
             layout = matrix(c(NA,       ends[1], NA,
                               training, NA,      ends[2]),
                             nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE),
             nCharNodes = 0, edge.color = "black", intercepts = FALSE,
             asize = 2.5, sizeMan = 11, sizeMan2 = 7, edge.label.cex = .8,
             mar = c(3, 2, 5, 9), DoNotPlot = TRUE) |>
    mark_sig(fit, std_type = TRUE) |>
    change_node_label(set_names(c(str_c("Engagement\n", wave),
                                  str_c("Well-being\nand agency\n", wave),
                                  "Training"),
                                c(ends, training)),
                      label.cex = 1) |>
    plot()
  fit_text(fit, title)
}

The measurement · Step 5

Step 5 · The same measurement over the waves all persons
What does the longitudinal model look like? The configural model, as its lavaan syntax; with four waves and the residuals linked across them, a path diagram would not stay readable (Chapter 7). title: 19. Training effects on the new structure
text:
19.5 The pathway: training, engagement, well-being
Which windows? The four of Chapter 12: the experimental group trains (Model 1, T0 to T1), durability from baseline (Model 2, T0 to T2), maintenance without new training (Model 3, T1 to T2, which controls for a state already after the training and is read with care), and the replication while the control group trains (Model 4, T2 to T3, with train_cg in place of train_eg).

The model · Steps 1 and 2

Step 1 · The model all persons
What is regressed on what? The scores at T1 on the training and on each other, controlling for both scores at T0:

m1_model <- "
  # a: the training -> Engagement
  engagement_T1 ~ a*train_eg + engagement_T0 + wellbeing_agency_T0
  # b: Engagement -> Well-being and agency, c: the training -> it
  wellbeing_agency_T1 ~ b*engagement_T1 + c*train_eg + engagement_T0 +
    wellbeing_agency_T0
  # the scores at T0 covary
  engagement_T0 ~~ wellbeing_agency_T0
  # the effects
  indirect := a*b
  direct   := c
  total    := c + a*b
"

m1_fit <- new_mediation$fit[[1]]   # fitted in the script

Next → Step 2, the path diagram: What does the model look like?


Step 2 · The path diagram all persons
What does the model look like?

m1_fit |>
  mediationPlot("Model 1: T0 to T1, the experimental group trains")








The diagram leaves out the two scores at T0, which both regressions control for. CFI and SRMR meet their criteria (CFI = .989, SRMR = .042), but the χ² test rejects the model (χ²(2) = 7.84, p = .020). Its two degrees of freedom are the relations of the training with the two scores at T0, which the model sets to zero. For Engagement this holds (r = -.05), but in January the experimental group stands lower on Well-being and agency (r = -.15; Step 2 of Well-being and agency in 19.3).

title: 22. Item-level Δd
text:
22.1 How each scale is examined
What is measured? For each of the 102 items (reverse-keyed items turned, Chapter 2), the repeated-measures Δd of Chapter 9: the d of the experimental group minus the d of the control group, each the mean change of the persons who answered at both waves divided by their standard deviation at the first wave, with a two-sided z-test. Three windows: while the experimental group trains (T0 to T1), its durability until September (T0 to T2), and while the control group trains (T2 to T3). In the last window the sign is turned, so that a positive value means a gain of the trained group in every window.
What happens to each scale? The same four steps, in the same order and in three parts: the items, their effects, and what follows. The diagram shows the path; the list below describes each step.





flowchart TB
  subgraph P0["the items"]
    direction LR
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br>the items"]
  end
  subgraph P1["the effects: both groups"]
    direction LR
    S2["<b>Step 2</b><br>Δd item by item"]
    S2 --> S3["<b>Step 3</b><br>the rank"]
  end
  V["<b>Step 4</b><br>what follows"]
  P0 --> P1
  P1 --> V
  classDef both fill:#f0eaf8,stroke:#8e6bbf,color:#1d1d1f
  classDef verdict fill:#ffffff,stroke:#1d1d1f,color:#1d1d1f
  class S1,S2,S3 both
  class V verdict
  style P0 fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a
  style P1 fill:#fafafa,stroke:#8a8a8a






The four steps in detail:
The items:

The items. Which questions make up the scale, in their wording, and which of them were asked the other way round (reverse-keyed).

The effects:

Δd item by item. The Δd and p of each item in the three windows; an item gains significantly when p < .05 and Δd > 0. With 102 items in a window, about five would reach p < .05 by chance alone, so the p-values describe the items; they are not corrected for testing many items.
The rank. The ranking index, the mean Δd of the two training windows (T0 to T1 and T2 to T3), and the rank of each item among all 102 (1 = the largest index). Marked are the items that gain significantly in both training windows.

What follows:

What follows. Where the items go in the post hoc structure of Chapters 15 to 18: set aside before the networks (Chapter 15: answers at the ceiling, negative wording, the block on attitudes toward women), unstable in the network (Chapter 16), set aside as redundant or for a weak discrimination (Chapter 17), or kept in the final pool (Chapter 17), on which Chapter 18 builds the composites and Chapter 19 the post hoc scores.

title: 22. Item-level Δd
text:
22.2 Data and tools
Which data? All questionnaires (df) and the wording of every item, loaded above, and the item pools of the post hoc structure: the pool before the networks and the stable items (Chapter 16), the items set aside as redundant or weakly discriminating, and the final pool (Chapter 17). Each item gets the step at which it leaves, or the final pool:

ega        <- readRDS("cache/structure_ega.rds")             # Chapter 16
pruned     <- readRDS("cache/structure_irt.rds")$pruned      # Chapter 17
final_pool <- readRDS("cache/structure_irt.rds")$final_pool  # Chapter 17

post_hoc <- tibble(item = item_names) |>
  left_join(select(pruned, item, poor, redundant), by = "item") |>
  mutate(post_hoc = case_when(
    !item %in% ega$pool   ~ "set aside before the networks (Chapter 15)",
    !item %in% ega$stable ~ "unstable in the network (Chapter 16)",
    redundant             ~ "redundant (Chapter 17)",
    poor                  ~ "weak discrimination (Chapter 17)",
    item %in% final_pool  ~ "final pool (Chapters 17 and 18)")) |>
  select(item, post_hoc)

post_hoc |>
  count(post_hoc)





post_hoc

No item leaves for a weak discrimination; the six items that Chapter 17 sets aside are all redundant.
Which tools? The Δd of Chapter 9 (delta_d()), and one small function for the figure at the end:

Effect sizesPathBoth windows



# Repeated-measures effect sizes (Chapters 9 and 14)
#
# d_rm(): the change of one group in one window, in standard deviations
# before the window (Morris & DeShon, 2002). Change, SD and standard error
# all come from the persons who answered at both waves.
# delta_d(): the difference experimental minus control, with a z-test.
# With sd_pre = "all", d is divided by the SD of every questionnaire of the
# group at the first wave, not only of the pairs; the standard error stays
# that of the pairs.

d_rm <- \(data, outcome, pre, post, group, sd_pre = "pairs") {
  waves <- data |>
    filter(condition == group, Occasion %in% c(pre, post)) |>
    select(id, Occasion, value = all_of(outcome))
  pairs <- waves |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = Occasion, values_from = value) |>
    drop_na()
  change <- mean(pairs[[post]] - pairs[[pre]])
  d <- change / sd(pairs[[pre]])
  r <- cor(pairs[[pre]], pairs[[post]])
  n <- nrow(pairs)
  se <- sqrt(2 * (1 - r) / n + d^2 / (2 * n))
  sd_all <- sd(waves$value[waves$Occasion == pre], na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(d = if (sd_pre == "all") change / sd_all else d, se = se, n = n)
}

delta_d <- \(data, pre, post, outcomes, sd_pre = "pairs") {
  map(outcomes, \(outcome) {
    eg <- d_rm(data, outcome, pre, post, "Experimental", sd_pre)
    cg <- d_rm(data, outcome, pre, post, "Control", sd_pre)
    tibble(outcome = outcome,
           d_EG = eg$d, n_EG = eg$n, d_CG = cg$d, n_CG = cg$n,
           delta_d = eg$d - cg$d, se = sqrt(eg$se^2 + cg$se^2))
  }) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(z = delta_d / se, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)))
}




# item numbers as "items 1 and 3", or "none"
numbered <- \(items) {
  if (length(items) == 0) return("none")
  numbers <- sort(as.integer(str_extract(items, "[0-9]+$")))
  str_c(if (length(numbers) == 1) "item " else "items ",
        str_flatten_comma(numbers, last = " and "))
}

# the path of a scale through the four steps, from the table of Δd above
# and the decisions of Chapters 15 to 17
item_path <- \(scale) {
  items <- scale_items[[scale]]
  effects <- item_effects |> filter(item %in% items)
  gains <- \(d, p) effects$item[p < .05 & d > 0]
  both <- intersect(gains(effects$delta_d_T0_T1, effects$p_T0_T1),
                    gains(effects$delta_d_T2_T3, effects$p_T2_T3))
  fates <- post_hoc |>
    filter(item %in% items) |>
    count(post_hoc) |>
    transmute(text = str_c(n, " ", str_remove(post_hoc, " \\(.*\\)$") |>
                             str_replace("^final pool", "in the final pool")))
  tribble(
    ~Step, ~Question, ~Result, ~Next,
    "2", "Which items gain while the experimental group trains?",
    numbered(gains(effects$delta_d_T0_T1, effects$p_T0_T1)), "the next window",
    "2", "Which items gain while the control group trains?",
    numbered(gains(effects$delta_d_T2_T3, effects$p_T2_T3)), "the rank",
    "3", "Which items gain in both windows, and how high do they rank?",
    str_c(numbered(both), "; best rank ", min(effects$rank), " of 102"),
    "what follows",
    "4", "Where do the items go in the post hoc structure?",
    str_flatten(fates$text, "; "), "")
}




# Δd of each item while the experimental group trains against Δd while
# the control group trains (sign turned), one panel per hypothesis block;
# filled: a significant gain of the trained group in both windows
plot_windows <- \(effects) {
  effects |>
    mutate(block = scales$block[match(str_remove(item, "[0-9]+$"),
                                      scales$scale)],
           both  = p_T0_T1 < .05 & delta_d_T0_T1 > 0 &
             p_T2_T3 < .05 & delta_d_T2_T3 > 0) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = delta_d_T0_T1, y = delta_d_T2_T3)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70", linewidth = .3) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70", linewidth = .3) +
    geom_point(aes(fill = both), shape = 21, size = 2.2,
               colour = "grey25") +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = \(d) filter(d, both),
                             aes(label = item), size = 3) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey15", `FALSE` = "white"),
                      guide = "none") +
    facet_wrap(~ block) +
    labs(x = "Δd while the experimental group trains (T0 to T1)",
         y = "Δd while the control group trains\n(T2 to T3, sign turned)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

  ~pre, ~post, ~window,   ~sign,
  "T0", "T1",  "T0_T1",   1,
  "T0", "T2",  "T0_T2",   1,
  "T2", "T3",  "T2_T3",  -1
) |>

    delta_d(df, a, b, item_names))) |>

  arrange(desc(training_mean)) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number(), .before = 1)

While the experimental group trains, 22 items gain significantly, while the control group trains 20: far more than chance alone would bring, about five of 102 tests in a window, in either direction. Item by item, however, the two windows agree only weakly (r = .27 over the 102 items). Of the 4 items with a significant gain of the trained group in both windows, 3 stay in the final pool of the post hoc structure.
Chapter 23 lists the software behind all analyses.

saveRDS(item_effects, "cache/item_effects.rds")
